a.states: For every number field E and all natural numbers m > 0 and b > 0, the text asserts that there is a natural number a > 0 that is coprime to b and has the following property. Every unit u of the ring of integers of E such that a divides u − 1 in that ring is the m-th power of a unit v of the same ring. The modulus a is a rational integer and may depend on E, m and b.
a.notation: ∀ number field E, ∀ m, b ≥ 1, ∃ a ≥ 1 with gcd(a, b) = 1 such that every u ∈ O_E^× with u ≡ 1 (mod a·O_E) lies in (O_E^×)^m
a.classical_name: Chevalley's theorem on units (congruence subgroup property of the unit group)
a.classical: Let K be a number field, S a finite set of places of K containing the archimedean ones, and n ≥ 1 an integer. Then there is an integral ideal 𝔪 prime to S such that every S-unit congruent to 1 modulo 𝔪 is the n-th power of an S-unit, so every subgroup of finite index in the S-units contains a congruence subgroup. The reference is C. Chevalley, Deux théorèmes d'arithmétique, Journal of the Mathematical Society of Japan 3, 1951.
differences: The Lean text concerns only the units of the ring of integers, whereas the S-unit form of the theorem concerns the S-units for an arbitrary finite set S of places.

The Lean text requires the modulus to be coprime to an arbitrary given integer b, which matches the S-unit form with S the places above the primes dividing b and claims more than the frequently quoted unit form that allows any modulus.

The Lean text takes the modulus to be a rational integer rather than an ideal, which loses nothing because an ideal prime to those places can be replaced by the positive generator of its intersection with ℤ, and that generator is coprime to b.
a.why: Published formulations differ between a unit version with an unrestricted modulus, against which the Lean text is stronger, and an S-unit version with a modulus prime to S, of which the Lean text is a special case.

b.states: For every number field E and all natural numbers m and b with 0 < m and 0 < b, there is a natural number a with 0 < a that is coprime to b. Every unit u of the ring of integers of E for which a divides u − 1 in that ring then equals v^m for some unit v of the ring of integers.
b.classical_name: Chevalley's theorem on congruence subgroups of the unit group of a number field (Chevalley 1951)
differences: The Lean statement demands that the modulus a be coprime to a freely chosen positive integer b, while the usual statement of Chevalley's theorem asserts only that some modulus exists.

The extra demand still holds, because the primes that the proof by Kummer theory and the Chebotarev density theorem puts into the modulus can be chosen outside any finite set of primes, so the strengthening keeps the statement true.
The modulus is a rational integer a instead of an ideal, which loses nothing because every nonzero ideal of the ring of integers contains a positive rational integer.

Only the subgroups of m-th powers of units appear, which loses nothing against the form with arbitrary subgroups of finite index, because a subgroup of index m in the abelian unit group contains every m-th power.

The Lean text concerns only the units of the ring of integers of E, while Chevalley's theorem in its published S-unit form concerns the S-units for any finite set S of places that contains the infinite ones.

The Lean text requires the modulus a to be coprime to an arbitrary positive integer b, which is what the S-unit form gives when S contains the primes above b, and which claims more than the unit form that allows any modulus.

The modulus is a positive rational integer a rather than an ideal, which loses nothing because the positive generator of the intersection with ℤ of an ideal prime to the primes above b is coprime to b.

Only the subgroup of m-th powers of units appears, which loses nothing against the form with arbitrary subgroups of finite index, because a subgroup of index k in the abelian unit group contains every k-th power.
check.note: The coprimality of the modulus to an arbitrary b is what Chevalley's S-unit theorem gives when S contains the primes above b, so the Lean text is that theorem restricted to units, and it is stronger only against the narrower unit form with a free modulus that B compares it with.

a.states: For all number fields K and L with L a Galois extension of K whose Galois group is cyclic, and for every nonzero a ∈ K, the text makes two assumptions. At every finite place v of K some element z of K_v ⊗_K L has norm a over the completion K_v, and at every infinite place v of K some element z of K_v ⊗_K L has norm a over K_v. The conclusion is that a = N_{L/K}(x) for some x ∈ L.
a.notation: L/K cyclic, a ∈ K^×, (∀ places v of K, a ∈ N_{K_v ⊗_K L / K_v}(K_v ⊗_K L)) ⟹ ∃ x ∈ L with N_{L/K}(x) = a
a.classical_name: Hasse norm theorem
a.classical: Let L/K be a cyclic extension of number fields. An element a ∈ K^× is the norm of an element of L^× if and only if, for every place v of K and a place w of L above v, it is the norm of an element of L_w^×. The reference is H. Hasse, Beweis eines Satzes und Widerlegung einer Vermutung über das allgemeine Normenrestsymbol, Nachrichten der Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen, 1931.
a.why: The norm from K_v ⊗_K L is the product of the norms from the completions L_w above v, and since L/K is Galois a norm from one L_w already gives a norm from the product, so the local hypotheses and the global conclusion match Hasse's theorem.

b.states: For all number fields K and L with L a Galois extension of K whose Galois group is cyclic, and for every nonzero a in K, an implication holds. Its first hypothesis is that for every finite place v of K some element z of the tensor product of the completion K_v with L over K has norm a over K_v. Its second hypothesis is the same condition at every infinite place of K with the archimedean completion. Its conclusion is that a equals the norm N_{L/K}(x) of some x in L.
b.classical_name: Hasse norm theorem
differences: The local condition is written as a norm from the algebra K_v ⊗_K L, which is the product of the completions L_w over the places w above v, and because these completions are isomorphic for a Galois extension the condition says exactly that a is a local norm from L_w, so the wording changes nothing.

The local condition is a norm from the algebra K_v ⊗_K L over K_v, which is the product of the completions L_w over the places w above v, and because these completions are isomorphic over K_v for a Galois extension and a is nonzero, the condition says exactly that a is a norm from L_w.
The Lean text states only that a local norm at every place is a global norm, and it leaves out the converse direction of the published equivalence, which is immediate.

a.states: For every number field F and all nonzero δ, x ∈ F, the text makes two assumptions. For every real embedding σ of F there are real numbers a, b with σ(x) = a² − σ(δ)b², and for every finite place v of F there are a, b in the completion F_v with x = a² − δb² in F_v. The conclusion is that x = a² − δb² for some a, b ∈ F. The complex places carry no condition, and none is needed because every complex number has this form.
a.notation: δ, x ∈ F^×, (∀ real σ, ∃ a, b ∈ ℝ with σ(x) = a² − σ(δ)b²) ∧ (∀ finite v, ∃ a, b ∈ F_v with x = a² − δb²) ⟹ ∃ a, b ∈ F with x = a² − δb²
a.classical_name: Hasse norm theorem for quadratic extensions
a.classical: Let F be a number field and δ ∈ F^× a non-square. An element x ∈ F^× is a norm from F(√δ), that is x = a² − δb² with a, b ∈ F, if and only if it is a norm from F_v(√δ) in every completion F_v. This is the case of degree 2 of Hasse's norm theorem and is equivalent to the Hasse–Minkowski theorem for the ternary form X² − δY² − xZ². The reference is H. Hasse, Beweis eines Satzes und Widerlegung einer Vermutung über das allgemeine Normenrestsymbol, Nachrichten der Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen, 1931.
differences: The Lean text treats only quadratic extensions F(√δ)/F, whereas Hasse's norm theorem covers every cyclic extension.
The Lean text also admits δ that is a square in F, a case that the classical statement excludes and in which the conclusion holds for every x.
a.vacuity: When δ is a square in F the conclusion holds for every x without using the local hypotheses, but in the main case where δ is not a square the statement has full content.
a.why: The expression a² − δb² is the norm form of F(√δ) over F and over each completion, and the real and finite places listed are exactly the places where the local norm condition can fail.

b.states: For every number field F and all nonzero δ and x in F, an implication holds. Its first hypothesis is that for every ring homomorphism σ from F to ℝ there are real a and b with σ x = a^2 − σ δ · b^2. Its second hypothesis is that for every finite place v of F there are a and b in the completion F_v with x = a^2 − δ · b^2 in F_v. Its conclusion is that there are a and b in F with x = a^2 − δ · b^2.
b.classical_name: Hasse norm theorem for quadratic extensions, equivalently the Hasse–Minkowski theorem for the ternary form X^2 − δY^2 − xZ^2
differences: The Lean statement covers only the extensions F(√δ)/F of degree at most 2, whose norm form is a^2 − δ b^2, while the Hasse norm theorem covers every cyclic extension of number fields.
Complex places carry no condition, which loses nothing because every complex number has the form a^2 − δ b^2 over ℂ.
When δ is a square in F the conclusion holds without any local hypothesis, and the Lean statement includes this trivial case without harm.
The Lean text covers only the extensions F(√δ)/F of degree at most 2 with norm form a² − δb², while Hasse's norm theorem covers every cyclic extension of number fields.
The complex places carry no condition, which loses nothing because every complex number has the form a² − δb² over ℂ.
The Lean text admits a δ that is a square in F, and in that case the conclusion holds for every x.
The Lean text states only the direction from local norms to a global norm, and the converse direction is immediate.
check.vacuity: No hypothesis is impossible to meet, and only in the subcase where δ is a square in F does the conclusion hold at once, so the statement keeps its full content for every non-square δ.

a.states: For every scheme S and every group scheme G over S whose structure morphism f is smooth, the text asserts that there is a group scheme G₀ over S and a homomorphism j from G₀ to G of group schemes over S whose underlying morphism of schemes is an open immersion. The image of j is exactly the set of points x of G that lie in the connected component of the unit point e(s) inside the fibre f⁻¹(s) over s = f(x), where the fibre carries the subspace topology. So j identifies G₀ with the open subgroup scheme formed by the identity components of all fibres.
a.notation: G → S smooth group scheme ⟹ ∃ group scheme G₀ over S and an open immersion homomorphism j from G₀ to G with j(G₀) = ⋃_{s ∈ S} (G_s)⁰, where (G_s)⁰ is the connected component of e(s) in f⁻¹(s)
a.classical_name: Openness of the identity component of a smooth group scheme
a.classical: Let G be a group scheme over a scheme S that is smooth over S. Then the union G⁰ of the identity components of the fibres G_s is an open subset of G, and with its open subscheme structure it is a subgroup scheme of G with connected fibres. The reference is M. Demazure and A. Grothendieck, Schémas en groupes I (SGA 3), Exposé VI_B, Théorème 3.10, 1970.
a.why: The image condition fixes the open set G⁰ point by point, an open subscheme is determined by its open set, and the topological fibre f⁻¹(s) is homeomorphic to the scheme-theoretic fibre G_s, so the Lean text says exactly that G⁰ is an open subgroup scheme.

b.states: For every scheme S in universe 0 and every group object G in the category of schemes over S whose structure morphism G → S is smooth, there exist a group object G₀ over S and a morphism j from G₀ to G over S. The morphism j is a homomorphism of group objects, and its underlying morphism of schemes is an open immersion. A point x of G lies in the image of j exactly when x lies in the connected component that contains the identity point e(s) inside the topological fibre of G over s, where s is the image of x in S.
b.classical_name: Existence of the open identity component G⁰ of a smooth group scheme (SGA 3, Exposé VI_B)
differences: The Lean statement asserts only that G₀ exists and leaves out the uniqueness that the published theorem includes, although uniqueness follows because an open subscheme is fixed by its underlying set and a group structure on it is fixed by the monomorphism j.

The Lean statement assumes that G → S is smooth, while SGA 3 needs only that G is locally of finite presentation over S with smooth fibres, so the Lean statement covers a narrower class of group schemes.
The fibre is taken as the subspace of points of G over s rather than as the scheme G_s, which changes nothing because the two spaces are homeomorphic.
Only schemes in universe 0 are covered.

The Lean text asserts only that G₀ and j exist and states no uniqueness, but uniqueness follows because j is an open immersion whose image the condition on points fixes, and j is a monomorphism of group objects.
The fibre is the set of points of G over s with the subspace topology rather than the scheme G_s, which changes nothing because the two spaces are homeomorphic.
The Lean text assumes that the structure morphism G → S is smooth, which is the hypothesis of the usual statement of the theorem.
Only schemes in universe 0 are covered.
check.note: The condition on points fixes the open set G⁰ as the union of the identity components of the fibres, and j makes this set an open subgroup scheme, which is the published conclusion for a smooth group scheme, while the uniqueness that B counts as missing follows from that condition, so the Lean text is not weaker.

a.states: Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff group with its Borel σ-algebra and a regular Haar measure μ that is both left and right invariant, and let π be a homomorphism from G into the bounded operators on a complex Hilbert space H. Assume that every π(g) is isometric, that every map g ↦ π(g)v is continuous, that the only closed invariant subspaces are 0 and H, and that some matrix coefficient g ↦ ⟨w₀, π(g)v₀⟩ with v₀ ≠ 0 and w₀ ≠ 0 lies in L²(μ). Then every matrix coefficient lies in L²(μ), and there is a real d > 0 such that for all v, w, v', w' the function ⟨w, π(g)v⟩·conj⟨w', π(g)v'⟩ is integrable with integral ⟨v', v⟩⟨w, w'⟩/d. The inner product here is conjugate linear in its first argument.
a.notation: π irreducible unitary, ∃ v₀, w₀ ≠ 0 with ⟨w₀, π(·)v₀⟩ ∈ L²(μ) ⟹ ∀ v, w, ⟨w, π(·)v⟩ ∈ L²(μ) and ∃ d > 0 with ∫_G ⟨w, π(g)v⟩ conj⟨w', π(g)v'⟩ dμ(g) = ⟨v', v⟩⟨w, w'⟩/d
a.classical_name: Schur orthogonality relations for square-integrable representations (Godement)
a.classical: Let G be a unimodular locally compact group and π an irreducible unitary representation of G on H. If one nonzero matrix coefficient g ↦ (π(g)u, v) is square integrable, then all of them are, and there is a constant d_π > 0, the formal degree, with ∫_G (π(g)u₁, v₁) conj(π(g)u₂, v₂) dg = d_π⁻¹ (u₁, u₂) conj(v₁, v₂) for all vectors. The reference is R. Godement, Sur les relations d'orthogonalité de V. Bargmann, Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences de Paris 225, 1947.
a.vacuity: The requirement that the Haar measure be right invariant can be met only on unimodular groups, which confines the statement to Godement's unimodular setting but leaves it with content, for example for every compact group.
a.why: After translating the inner product convention, with (x, y) in the classical notation equal to ⟨y, x⟩ in the Lean notation, the hypotheses and the orthogonality formula coincide term by term with Godement's theorem.

b.states: Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group with its Borel σ-algebra and a regular Haar measure μ that is also right invariant, and let π be a homomorphism from G into the bounded operators on a complex Hilbert space H. Assume that every π g preserves norms, that g ↦ π g v is continuous for every v, that the only closed π-invariant subspaces are 0 and H, and that one matrix coefficient g ↦ ⟪w₀, π g v₀⟫ with v₀ ≠ 0 and w₀ ≠ 0 lies in L^2(μ). Then every matrix coefficient g ↦ ⟪w, π g v⟫ lies in L^2(μ), and there is a real d > 0 such that for all v, w, v', w' in H the function g ↦ ⟪w, π g v⟫ · conj ⟪w', π g v'⟫ is integrable with integral ⟪v', v⟫ · ⟪w, w'⟫ / d. The inner product is conjugate linear in its first argument, as in Mathlib.
b.classical_name: Schur orthogonality relations for square-integrable representations (Godement's theorem on the formal degree)
differences: The Lean statement gives only the relation for a single representation and omits the second published relation, which says that the matrix coefficients of two inequivalent square-integrable representations are orthogonal in L^2(G).
Requiring μ to be both left and right invariant restricts G to unimodular groups, which is also the setting of Godement's theorem, so this restriction loses nothing against that version.
Unitarity is expressed as norm preservation of every π g, which is equivalent because π g has the inverse π g⁻¹.

With the inner product conjugate linear in its first argument, the right side ⟪v', v⟫ · ⟪w, w'⟫ / d is the published d⁻¹ ⟨v, v'⟩ conj ⟨w, w'⟩ with the inner product linear in its first argument, so the formulas agree.

The Lean text treats a single representation π and leaves out the second orthogonality relation, which says that the matrix coefficients of two inequivalent square-integrable irreducible representations are orthogonal in L²(G).
The Haar measure is required to be both left and right invariant, which confines G to unimodular groups, the setting of Godement's theorem.
Unitarity is expressed as norm preservation of every π g, which is equivalent because π g has the inverse π g⁻¹.

With the inner product conjugate linear in its first argument, the right side ⟪v', v⟫ · ⟪w, w'⟫ / d equals the published d⁻¹ (v, v') conj(w, w') with the inner product linear in its first argument, so the formulas agree.
check.note: The Lean text has only one representation and so cannot express the orthogonality of the coefficients of inequivalent representations that the Schur orthogonality relations of Godement also assert, which makes it one of the two published relations and therefore weaker, while A compared it with the first relation alone.

a.states: For every prime l and every number field K that is abelian over ℚ and contains a primitive l-th root of unity, or a primitive fourth root of unity when l = 2, the text asserts that there is a natural number r with the following property. For every n and every field K' generated over K by a primitive l^n-th root of unity, the quotient of the class group of K' by its subgroup of l-th powers has at most l^r elements. So the l-rank of the class groups along the tower K(μ_{l^n}) is bounded independently of n.
a.notation: ∀ l prime, ∀ K/ℚ abelian with μ_l ⊂ K (μ_4 ⊂ K if l = 2), ∃ r, ∀ n ≥ 0, |Cl(K(μ_{l^n})) / Cl(K(μ_{l^n}))^l| ≤ l^r
a.classical_name: Ferrero–Washington theorem
a.classical: For every abelian number field K and every prime p, the Iwasawa μ-invariant of the cyclotomic ℤ_p-extension of K vanishes. By Iwasawa's theorem on the growth of class groups this is equivalent to the boundedness of the p-rank of the class groups of the layers of that extension. The reference is B. Ferrero and L. C. Washington, The Iwasawa invariant μ_p vanishes for abelian number fields, Annals of Mathematics 109, 1979.
differences: The Lean text states that the l-rank of the class groups is bounded instead of stating μ = 0, and the two are equivalent only through Iwasawa's structure theory of the class groups in a ℤ_l-extension.

The Lean text restricts the base field to abelian fields containing μ_l, or μ_4 when l = 2, while the published theorem covers every abelian field, although the general case follows from the restricted one because the μ-invariant of K is at most that of the abelian field K(μ_l) or K(i).

The Lean text indexes the tower by the fields K(μ_{l^n}), which under the root-of-unity hypothesis are the layers of the cyclotomic ℤ_l-extension of K, with a shift of numbering and repetitions for small n.
a.why: The relation rests on the standard equivalence between bounded l-rank and μ = 0 and on the standard reduction to fields containing μ_l, which are not part of the published statement itself.

b.states: For every prime l and every number field K that is an abelian Galois extension of ℚ and contains a primitive root of unity of order 4 when l = 2 and of order l otherwise, there is a natural number r with a uniform bound. For every natural number n and every number field K' that is a cyclotomic extension of K generated by the l^n-th roots of unity, the quotient of the class group of K' by its subgroup of l-th powers has at most l^r elements. This says that the l-rank of the class group stays bounded along the tower of fields K(μ_{l^n}).
b.classical_name: Ferrero–Washington theorem (vanishing of the Iwasawa μ-invariant for abelian number fields)
differences: The published theorem says that the Iwasawa μ-invariant of the cyclotomic ℤ_l-extension of an abelian number field vanishes, while the Lean statement bounds the l-rank of the class groups in the layers K(μ_{l^n}), and the two are equivalent by Iwasawa's structure theory of class groups in ℤ_l-extensions.

The Lean statement covers only abelian fields K that already contain the l-th roots of unity, or the 4th roots of unity for l = 2, so that the fields K(μ_{l^n}) are the layers of the cyclotomic ℤ_l-extension of K.
The general abelian field follows from this case by passing from K to K(μ_l) or K(μ_4) and comparing class groups by the norm map, but the Lean statement does not state the general case.

The Lean text bounds the l-rank of the class groups through the order of their quotient by l-th powers instead of stating that the μ-invariant vanishes, and the two are equivalent by Iwasawa's theory of class groups in ℤ_l-extensions.
The Lean text covers only abelian fields K that contain a primitive l-th root of unity, or a primitive fourth root of unity when l = 2, while the published theorem covers every abelian number field.
Under that root-of-unity hypothesis the fields K(μ_{l^n}) are the layers of the cyclotomic ℤ_l-extension of K, with a shift of numbering and repetitions for small n.

a.states: For every finite group G and every finite-dimensional complex representation ρ of G on V, the text asserts that there are finitely many subgroups H_1, …, H_r of G, homomorphisms χ_i from H_i to ℂ^× and integers c_i such that tr ρ(g) − dim V = Σ_i c_i (Ind_{H_i}^G χ_i(g) − Ind_{H_i}^G 1(g)) for every g ∈ G. The project's induced function is the usual one, Ind_H^G f(g) = |H|⁻¹ Σ f(x⁻¹gx) over the x ∈ G with x⁻¹gx ∈ H. So the virtual character χ_ρ − (dim ρ)·1_G of degree zero is an integral combination of the virtual characters Ind_H^G(χ − 1_H) with χ linear.
a.notation: χ_ρ − (dim ρ)·1_G = Σ_{i=1}^r c_i Ind_{H_i}^G(χ_i − 1_{H_i}) with H_i ≤ G, χ_i ∈ Hom(H_i, ℂ^×), c_i ∈ ℤ
a.classical_name: Brauer's induction theorem in degree-zero form
a.classical: For a finite group G, every virtual character of degree zero is a ℤ-linear combination of virtual characters Ind_H^G(λ − 1_H), where H runs over subgroups of G, which may even be taken elementary, and λ over one-dimensional characters of H. It is a corollary of Brauer's theorem that every character is an integral combination of characters induced from linear characters of elementary subgroups. The reference is J. Martinet, Character theory and Artin L-functions, in A. Fröhlich (ed.), Algebraic Number Fields, Academic Press, 1977.
differences: The Lean text treats the degree-zero virtual character χ_ρ − (dim ρ)·1_G of a genuine representation rather than an arbitrary virtual character of degree zero, although every virtual character of degree zero is a difference of two such characters, so the general statement follows by subtraction.
The Lean text allows the subgroups H_i to be arbitrary, while the sharper published form uses only elementary subgroups.
a.why: The induction formula in the dossier is the standard one, and the statement is the degree-zero corollary of Brauer's theorem restricted to characters of representations.

b.states: For every finite group G and every finite dimensional complex representation ρ of G on V, there are a natural number r, subgroups H_1, …, H_r of G, homomorphisms χ_i from H_i to ℂˣ and integers c_i with one identity. For every g in G, the trace of ρ(g) minus the dimension of V equals the sum over i of c_i times the induced function of χ_i at g minus the induced function of the constant 1 at g. The project's indFun computes the induced class function by the usual formula (1/|H|) Σ_{x ∈ G, x⁻¹gx ∈ H} f(x⁻¹gx).
b.classical_name: Brauer's induction theorem in its degree-zero form (every virtual character of degree 0 is an integral combination of Ind_H^G(χ − 1_H) with χ of degree 1)
differences: The Lean statement is written for χ_ρ − dim ρ with ρ a genuine representation, and these differences span all virtual characters of degree zero, so nothing is lost by the wording.
Brauer's theorem itself also lets the subgroups be chosen elementary, and the Lean statement does not claim this.

The Lean text treats the degree-zero virtual characters χ_ρ − dim ρ of genuine representations, and since every virtual character of degree zero is a difference of two of these, the general degree-zero statement follows by subtraction.
The Lean text allows arbitrary subgroups H_i and does not claim the sharper form in which the subgroups are elementary.
The project's indFun is the usual formula for the induced class function, |H|⁻¹ times the sum of f(x⁻¹gx) over the x in G with x⁻¹gx in H.
check.note: The restriction to genuine representations loses nothing because subtraction recovers every virtual character of degree zero, so the Lean text is equivalent to the degree-zero form of Brauer's theorem with arbitrary subgroups that both readers name, and only the refinement to elementary subgroups is absent.

a.states: For every algebraically closed field k, every group scheme B over Spec k that is an abelian scheme in the project's sense, meaning commutative, smooth, proper and geometrically connected, and smooth of relative dimension g, and every natural number n that is nonzero in k, the text asserts that the k-points x of B with x^n = 1 number exactly n^{2g}. The k-points are the sections Spec k → B with their group structure. The condition that n is nonzero in k means that n ≥ 1 and the characteristic of k does not divide n.
a.notation: A/k abelian variety of dimension g, k algebraically closed, char k ∤ n ⟹ #A[n](k) = n^{2g}
a.classical_name: Structure of the n-torsion of an abelian variety
a.classical: Let A be an abelian variety of dimension g over an algebraically closed field k and n an integer not divisible by the characteristic of k. Then multiplication by n is a separable isogeny of degree n^{2g}, and the group A[n] of n-torsion points is isomorphic to (ℤ/nℤ)^{2g}. The reference is D. Mumford, Abelian Varieties, Oxford University Press, 1970, §4 and §6.
differences: The Lean text asserts only that the n-torsion has n^{2g} points, while the published theorem also determines its group structure as (ℤ/nℤ)^{2g}.

The project's definition of an abelian scheme includes commutativity of the group law as a hypothesis, which classically follows from properness and connectedness, so this extra hypothesis excludes no abelian variety.
a.why: Over an algebraically closed field the project's abelian scheme of relative dimension g is an abelian variety of dimension g, and the count n^{2g} is the cardinality part of Mumford's description of A[n].

b.states: For every algebraically closed field k, every group object B over Spec k and all natural numbers g and n, an implication holds. Its hypotheses are that B is an abelian scheme in the project's sense, which means commutative, smooth, proper and with geometrically connected fibres, that B → Spec k is smooth of relative dimension g, and that n is nonzero in k. Its conclusion is that the set of k-points x of B with x^n = 1 has exactly n^(2 * g) elements. The k-points are the sections from the unit object Spec k to B, with the group law that the group object induces.
b.classical_name: Structure of the n-torsion of an abelian variety, A[n](k) has n^{2g} elements when the characteristic of k does not divide n (Mumford, Abelian Varieties)
differences: The Lean statement gives the cardinality n^{2g} and not the group isomorphism A[n] ≅ (ℤ/nℤ)^{2g}, but because it holds for every n that is nonzero in k the isomorphism follows from the cardinalities.
Commutativity is among the hypotheses, which costs nothing because every abelian variety is commutative.

Then there is a matrix P over E with nonzero determinant and G' = Pᵀ G σ(P). So two nondegenerate Hermitian forms that are isometric at every place of F are isometric over E.

a.classical: Let E/F be a quadratic extension of number fields with nontrivial automorphism σ. Two nondegenerate σ-Hermitian forms over E are isometric if and only if they are isometric over F_v ⊗_F E for every place v of F, and equivalently such forms are classified by rank, determinant modulo norms and the signatures at the real places of F that do not split in E. The reference is W. Landherr, Äquivalenz Hermitescher Formen über einem beliebigen algebraischen Zahlkörper, Abhandlungen aus dem Mathematischen Seminar der Universität Hamburg 11, 1935.

Then there is a matrix P over E with nonzero determinant and G' = Pᵀ · G · σ(P). This says that two nondegenerate hermitian forms over E/F that are isometric at every completion are isometric over E.

a.states: For every finite field k and every natural number n, the text claims that there are a dimension d and a representation ρ of GL_{n+1}(k) on ℂ^d that is irreducible and cuspidal. For monotone b these elements u form the unipotent radical N_P of the standard parabolic subgroup P whose diagonal blocks are the level sets of b, and the nonconstant b give exactly the proper standard parabolic subgroups. The definition therefore says that ρ has no nonzero N_P-invariant vector for any proper standard parabolic subgroup P.

a.states: Fix a CM field E with complex conjugation x ↦ x̄, a number r, an r×r matrix G over E with G_ba = Ḡ_ab and det G ≠ 0, a nonzero fractional ideal c, a nonzero integral ideal 𝔪 and a finite index set ι, and let h(y, z) = Σ_{a,b} y_a G_ab z̄_b be the Hermitian form of G on E^r. The text considers any set 𝓛 of pairs (L, x) where L is an O_E-lattice in E^r, meaning a finitely generated O_E-submodule that spans E^r, and x = (x_i)_{i∈ι} is a family of vectors of L, and it assumes that for every pair the set {y ∈ E^r | h(y, z) ∈ O_E for all z ∈ L} equals cL. It claims that 𝓛 has a finite subset S such that every (L, x) in 𝓛 is carried to some (L′, x′) in S by a γ ∈ GL_r(E) that preserves h, maps L onto L′ and satisfies γx_i ≡ x′_i modulo 𝔪L′ for every i.
a.notation: E CM, G = Ḡᵀ ∈ GL_r(E), c ≠ 0, 𝔪 ≠ 0, ι finite, 𝓛 ⊆ {(L, x) | L lattice in E^r with L^# = cL, x ∈ L^ι} ⇒ ∃ S ⊆ 𝓛 finite, ∀ (L, x) ∈ 𝓛, ∃ (L′, x′) ∈ S, ∃ γ ∈ U(G)(E) with γL = L′ and γx_i ≡ x′_i mod 𝔪L′ for all i
a.classical_name: Finiteness of class numbers for Hermitian lattices (Borel, Borel and Harish-Chandra)
a.classical: For a reductive group 𝐆 over a number field F and an open compact subgroup K of 𝐆(𝔸_f), the double coset space 𝐆(F)∖𝐆(𝔸_f)/K is finite. Applied to the unitary group of a Hermitian space over a CM field, this says that every genus of Hermitian lattices, also with a level structure, contains finitely many isometry classes, and the local classification of Hermitian lattices shows that the lattices with a fixed dual relation L^# = cL form finitely many genera. The reference is A. Borel, Some finiteness properties of adele groups over number fields, Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS 16, 1963.
differences: The Lean text concerns only unitary groups of Hermitian forms over CM fields, while Borel's theorem holds for every reductive group over a number field.
The Lean family 𝓛 may meet several genera, so the Lean claim also uses the finiteness of the number of local isometry classes of lattices with L^# = cL, which Borel's theorem does not contain.
The Lean text adds a level structure, a finite family of vectors of L taken modulo 𝔪L, which corresponds to a smaller open compact subgroup.
The Lean text measures duality with the O_E-valued form h itself rather than with its trace to ℚ, which is one of the two usual conventions.
a.vacuity: None found, since for example the identity matrix with c = O_E and the lattice O_E^r meets every hypothesis.
a.why: The Lean claim is true and follows from Borel's finiteness theorem together with the local finiteness of genera, but it is a corollary of that theorem rather than a published statement of the same shape.

b.states: Fix a CM field E, a natural number r, an r × r matrix G over E with conj(G_ab) = G_ba and nonzero determinant, a nonzero fractional ideal c, a nonzero integral ideal 𝔪 and a finite index type ι, and let 𝓛 be any set of pairs (L, x), with L an 𝓞_E-submodule of E^r and x a family of vectors indexed by ι. The statement assumes three things for each pair. L is finitely generated and spans E^r, the set of vectors v with h_G(v, y) an algebraic integer for all y in L equals c·L, where h_G(v, y) = Σ_a Σ_b v_a G_ab conj(y_b), and every x_i lies in L. It concludes that 𝓛 has a finite subset S such that for every pair (L, x) in 𝓛 there are a pair (L', x') in S and a matrix γ in GL_r(E) that preserves h_G, maps L onto L' and satisfies γx_i − x'_i ∈ 𝔪L' for every i.
b.classical_name: Finiteness of the class number of hermitian lattices, in the form with level structure (Borel's finiteness theorem applied to the unitary group)
differences: The Lean text treats only CM fields with their complex conjugation, while finiteness of class numbers holds for hermitian forms over any quadratic extension of number fields and for reductive groups in general.

The Lean text selects lattices by the condition that their dual equals c·L for one fixed fractional ideal c. This family can meet several genera, so the statement needs both the finiteness of the number of such genera and the finiteness of the classes in each genus.

The Lean text adds a level structure, a finite family of vectors of L compared modulo 𝔪L, which the plain class number statement lacks. This adds only finitely many choices per class because L/𝔪L is finite.
The representatives must lie in the given set 𝓛, which is equivalent to finiteness of the classes that 𝓛 meets.

The Lean text concerns only Hermitian forms over CM fields with their complex conjugation, while Borel's finiteness theorem holds for every reductive group over a number field and the finiteness of Hermitian class numbers holds over every quadratic extension of number fields.

The Lean family 𝓛 is cut out by the dual condition L^# = cL for one fixed fractional ideal c, measured with the O_E-valued form h_G itself, and such a family can meet several genera, so the Lean claim also needs the finiteness of the number of local isometry classes of such lattices.

The Lean text adds a level structure, a finite family of vectors of L compared modulo 𝔪L, which corresponds to a smaller open compact subgroup and adds only finitely many choices per class because L/𝔪L is finite.
The Lean text takes the representatives from the given set 𝓛, which is equivalent to the finiteness of the classes that 𝓛 meets.

a.states: The text is the conjunction of a local claim and a global claim, and in both a nonsingular matrix G′ is called congruent to G when G′ = Pᵀ G P̄ for some invertible P, with the bar standing for the nontrivial automorphism. The local claim says that for every nonarchimedean local field K with 2 ≠ 0, every quadratic extension L of K with a nontrivial K-automorphism σ, and all nonsingular r×r matrices G, G′ over L with σ(G_ab) = G_ba and σ(G′_ab) = G′_ba, the matrix G′ is congruent to G if and only if det G / det G′ equals x·σ(x) for some x ∈ L. The global claim says that for every CM field E with maximal real subfield F and all nonsingular Hermitian r×r matrices G, G′ over E, if G′ is congruent to G over F_v ⊗_F E for every finite place v of F, with an invertible P over that ring, and if for every embedding τ of E into ℂ the complex Hermitian matrix G′^τ equals Qᵀ G^τ Q̄ for some invertible complex Q, then G′ is congruent to G over E.
a.notation: (∀ K nonarchimedean local with 2 ≠ 0, ∀ L/K quadratic with Gal(L/K) = {1, σ}, ∀ nonsingular σ-Hermitian G, G′ ∈ M_r(L), G′ ≅ G ⇔ det G / det G′ ∈ N_{L/K}(L^×)) ∧ (∀ E CM with F = E⁺, ∀ nonsingular Hermitian G, G′ ∈ M_r(E), [G′ ≅ G over F_v ⊗_F E for all finite v and G′^τ ≅ G^τ over ℂ for all τ] ⇒ G′ ≅ G over E), where G′ ≅ G means G′ = Pᵀ G P̄ for an invertible P
a.classical_name: Local classification of Hermitian forms and Landherr's Hasse principle
a.classical: Over a nonarchimedean local field K of characteristic different from 2 and a quadratic extension L of K, two nondegenerate Hermitian forms are isometric if and only if they have the same dimension and their determinants agree modulo norms from L. Landherr's theorem says that two nondegenerate Hermitian forms over a quadratic extension of number fields are isometric if and only if they are isometric at every place of the base field, so they are classified by dimension, determinant and the signatures at the real places that do not split. The reference is W. Scharlau, Quadratic and Hermitian Forms, Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften 270, Springer 1985, Chapter 10.
differences: The global part is stated only for a CM field over its maximal real subfield, while Landherr's theorem holds for every quadratic extension of number fields.
The global part states only the Hasse principle and not the resulting classification by dimension, determinant and signatures.
At the archimedean places the Lean text asks for a complex congruence G′^τ = Qᵀ G^τ Q̄ for each embedding τ, which by Sylvester's law of inertia is the usual condition that the signatures agree.
a.vacuity: None found, since 2 ≠ 0 makes every quadratic extension Galois, so a nontrivial σ always exists, and every hypothesis of the global part is met by G′ = G.
a.why: Both parts translate directly into the standard local classification and Landherr's theorem, and the restriction to CM fields is the only narrowing.

b.states: The proposition is a conjunction of two statements. The first concerns a nonarchimedean local field K with 2 ≠ 0, a quadratic extension L of K with a K-automorphism σ ≠ 1, a natural number r and two r × r matrices G and G' over L that are hermitian for σ and have nonzero determinants. It says that G' = Pᵀ G σ(P) for some P with nonzero determinant exactly when det G / det G' = x σ(x) for some x in L. The second concerns a CM field E with maximal real subfield F and two hermitian r × r matrices G and G' over E with nonzero determinants. Suppose G and G' are congruent in this sense over F_v ⊗_F E for every finite place v of F, with conjugation acting on the factor E and P having unit determinant, and suppose they are congruent over ℂ via complex conjugation after every embedding of E into ℂ. Then G' = Pᵀ G conj(P) for some P over E with nonzero determinant.
b.classical_name: Landherr's theorem (the Hasse principle for hermitian forms), together with the classification of hermitian forms over local fields by their determinant (Landherr 1936, Jacobowitz 1962)
differences: The global part is stated only for a CM field over its maximal real subfield, while Landherr's Hasse principle holds for every quadratic extension of number fields.

The local part is stated for every nonarchimedean local field with 2 ≠ 0. This includes local fields of odd positive characteristic, which lie beyond the p-adic fields of Landherr, though the same classification by determinant is standard there.
The archimedean local condition is written as congruence over ℂ after each embedding, which amounts to equal signatures at every real place of the maximal real subfield.
The finite local conditions are written over F_v ⊗_F E, so split places enter as F_v × F_v, where forms of equal rank are always congruent.
The Lean text joins the local classification and the global principle in one conjunction. It leaves out the easy converse that global congruence implies local congruence.
The global part is stated only for a CM field over its maximal real subfield, while Landherr's Hasse principle holds for every quadratic extension of number fields.
The global part states only the direction from local congruence to global congruence and leaves out the easy converse and the resulting classification by dimension, determinant and signatures.

The archimedean condition is written as a congruence G′^τ = Qᵀ G^τ Q̄ over ℂ for each embedding τ of E, which by Sylvester's law of inertia amounts to equal signatures at every real place of the maximal real subfield.
The finite local conditions are written over F_v ⊗_F E with a matrix P of unit determinant, so a split place enters through F_v × F_v, where Hermitian forms of equal rank are always congruent.
The local part covers every nonarchimedean local field with 2 ≠ 0, which includes the local fields of odd positive characteristic, where the same classification by determinant holds.

a.states: For every imaginary quadratic field K, written as a totally complex number field of degree 2 with a chosen embedding of K into ℂ, every nonzero fractional ideal 𝔞 of O_K and every lattice Λ ⊂ ℂ given by a period pair whose point set is the image of 𝔞, the text makes two claims about the j-invariant of the curve y² = x³ − (g₂(Λ)/4)x − g₃(Λ)/4. The first claim is that j(Λ) = 1728 g₂³/(g₂³ − 27g₃²) is algebraic over K. The second claim is that the orbit of j(Λ) under all field automorphisms of ℂ that fix K equals the set of j-invariants of all lattices that are images of nonzero fractional ideals of O_K. Mathlib's j-invariant presupposes that the discriminant g₂³ − 27g₃² is invertible, and the dossier does not show the instance that supplies this, but the discriminant of a lattice is never zero, so the Lean j agrees with the classical one.
a.notation: K imaginary quadratic, K ↪ ℂ, 𝔞 a nonzero fractional ideal of O_K, Λ = 𝔞 ⊂ ℂ ⇒ j(Λ) algebraic over K and {σ(j(Λ)) | σ ∈ Aut(ℂ/K)} = {j(𝔟) | 𝔟 a nonzero fractional ideal of O_K}
a.classical_name: Main theorem of complex multiplication for j-invariants (Weber, Hasse)
a.classical: Let K be an imaginary quadratic field and E an elliptic curve over ℂ with endomorphism ring O_K, for example ℂ/𝔞 for a fractional ideal 𝔞 of O_K. Then j(E) is an algebraic integer, K(j(E)) is the Hilbert class field of K, the degree of K(j(E)) over K is the class number h_K, and the conjugates of j(E) over K are exactly the numbers j(ℂ/𝔟) for 𝔟 running over the ideal classes of K. The reference is J. H. Silverman, Advanced Topics in the Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 151, Springer 1994, Chapter II, Theorems 4.3 and 6.1.
differences: The Lean text claims only that j(𝔞) is algebraic over K, while the published theorem says that it is an algebraic integer.
The Lean text does not claim that the degree of K(j(𝔞)) over K equals the class number or that K(j(𝔞)) is the Hilbert class field.
The Lean text describes the conjugates as an orbit under the automorphisms of ℂ over K instead of under Gal(K̄/K), which gives the same set for an algebraic number.

The Lean set of j-values runs over all nonzero fractional ideals rather than over a set of representatives of the ideal classes, which gives the same set because ideals in one class give homothetic lattices.
a.why: The dossier's definitions give the standard lattice j-invariant and the standard set of j-invariants with complex multiplication by O_K, and the orbit claim is part (c) of Silverman's Theorem II.4.3.

b.states: Take a number field K that is totally complex of degree 2 over ℚ, which makes it an imaginary quadratic field, together with a chosen embedding into ℂ. For every invertible fractional ideal 𝔞 of K and every period pair L whose lattice is the image of 𝔞 in ℂ, two things hold. The j-invariant of the curve y² = x³ − (g₂(L)/4)x − g₃(L)/4, which equals 1728 g₂³/(g₂³ − 27 g₃²), is algebraic over K. The orbit of this j-invariant under the field automorphisms of ℂ that fix K equals the set of j-invariants of the same curves for the lattices of all invertible fractional ideals of K.
b.classical_name: Main theorem of complex multiplication for j-invariants, that j(𝔞) is algebraic and its conjugates over K are exactly the values j(𝔟) for the ideal classes of K (Weber, Hasse)

a_errors: A says that the Lean text does not claim that the degree of K(j(𝔞)) over K equals the class number, but the Lean equality MulAction.orbit (ℂ ≃ₐ[K] ℂ) (latticeCurve L).j = idealInvariants K fixes that degree as the number of distinct values in idealInvariants K, which is the class number because ideals give the same j-invariant exactly when they lie in the same class.
differences: The Lean text claims only that j(𝔞) is algebraic over K and leaves out that j(𝔞) is an algebraic integer and that K(j(𝔞)) is the Hilbert class field of K, which are separate parts of the main theorem of complex multiplication.

The Lean text describes the conjugates of j(𝔞) as its orbit under the automorphisms of ℂ over K instead of under Gal(K̄/K), which gives the same set for an algebraic number because every K-embedding of K(j(𝔞)) into ℂ extends to an automorphism of ℂ.

The Lean set idealInvariants K runs over all invertible fractional ideals rather than over representatives of the ideal classes, which gives the same set because ideals in one class give homothetic lattices with the same j-invariant.
The Lean curve y² = x³ − (g₂/4)x − g₃/4 is isomorphic to y² = 4x³ − g₂x − g₃, and its j-invariant is the classical 1728 g₂³/(g₂³ − 27g₃²).
check.note: I judge it the same because the name and the Lean text both target the statement that the j-invariants of the ideal classes of K form one Galois orbit over K, which the Lean text states exactly, while integrality and the Hilbert class field, on which A bases its verdict of weaker, are separate parts of the main theorem of complex multiplication.

a.states: Fix a nonarchimedean local field F with 2 ≠ 0, a finite-dimensional F-vector space W with its natural topology, a nondegenerate alternating bilinear form B on W and a continuous nontrivial additive character ψ of F with values in ℂ^×. The text makes two claims about the Heisenberg group H = W × F with product (w, t)(w′, t′) = (w + w′, t + t′ + B(w, w′)/2) and the product topology. The first claim is that some complex representation of H is smooth, meaning that every vector has an open stabiliser, is algebraically irreducible and has central character ψ, meaning that (0, t) acts as multiplication by ψ(t). The second claim is that any two such representations are isomorphic.
a.notation: ∀ F nonarchimedean local with 2 ≠ 0, ∀ (W, B) finite-dimensional symplectic over F, ∀ ψ nontrivial continuous character of F, ∃! (up to isomorphism) smooth irreducible ρ of H(W, B) with ρ(0, t) = ψ(t)·id
a.classical_name: Stone–von Neumann theorem for the Heisenberg group over a p-adic field
a.classical: Let F be a nonarchimedean local field of characteristic different from 2, W a symplectic space over F and H(W) its Heisenberg group. For each nontrivial character ψ of F there is, up to isomorphism, exactly one smooth irreducible representation of H(W) with central character ψ, and it is admissible and realised by the Schrödinger model. The reference is C. Mœglin, M.-F. Vignéras and J.-L. Waldspurger, Correspondances de Howe sur un corps p-adique, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1291, Springer 1987, Chapter 2.
differences: The original theorem of Stone and von Neumann concerns real symplectic spaces and unitary representations on Hilbert spaces, and the Lean text states only its p-adic smooth analogue.

The Lean text allows any continuous character ψ with values in ℂ^×, while the published theorem takes unitary characters, and the two agree because F is a union of compact open subgroups, so every continuous character of F is unitary and trivial on some open subgroup.
The Lean text omits the admissibility of the representation and its explicit Schrödinger model.
a.why: The project's Heisenberg group, smoothness condition and central character condition are the standard ones, and the existence and uniqueness claims match the p-adic theorem.

b.states: Take a nonarchimedean local field F with 2 ≠ 0, a finite-dimensional F-vector space W with its module topology, an alternating nondegenerate bilinear form B on W and a continuous nontrivial additive character ψ of F with complex values. The Heisenberg group is the set W × F with product (w, t)(w', t') = (w + w', t + t' + B(w, w')/2) and the product topology. There is a representation of this group on a complex vector space that is smooth, which means that every vector has an open stabilizer, that is irreducible, and that has central character ψ, which means that (0, t) acts as multiplication by ψ(t). Any two representations with these three properties are isomorphic.
b.classical_name: Stone–von Neumann theorem for the Heisenberg group over a nonarchimedean local field

differences: The Lean text states the smooth version over a nonarchimedean local field with 2 ≠ 0, which is the theorem in Mœglin, Vignéras and Waldspurger, and not the original theorem of Stone and von Neumann about unitary representations of the real Heisenberg group on Hilbert spaces.

The Lean text allows any continuous nontrivial character ψ of F with complex values, which agrees with the unitary characters of the published theorem because F is a union of compact open subgroups, so every continuous character of F is unitary.
The Lean text leaves out the admissibility of the representation and its explicit Schrödinger model.

a.states: For every commutative ring R with an ideal I such that I² = 0, every commutative ring R₀ with a surjective ring map π from R to R₀ whose kernel is I, and every group scheme A₀ over Spec R₀ that is an abelian scheme, the text claims that there are a group scheme A over Spec R and a morphism i from A₀ to A with three properties. The square formed by i, the two structure maps and Spec π is a pullback, so A₀ is the base change of A to Spec R₀, the map i respects the group laws on points with values in every scheme over Spec R₀, and A is an abelian scheme. The project defines an abelian scheme as a group object in schemes over the base that is commutative, smooth, proper and geometrically connected. In words, every abelian scheme over R₀ lifts to an abelian scheme over the square-zero thickening R.
a.notation: ∀ R, ∀ I ⊆ R with I² = 0, R₀ = R/I, ∀ A₀ abelian scheme over Spec R₀, ∃ A abelian scheme over Spec R with A ×_{Spec R} Spec R₀ ≅ A₀ as group schemes
a.classical_name: Grothendieck's theorem on infinitesimal lifting of abelian schemes
a.classical: Let R be a ring, I ⊆ R a nilpotent ideal and A₀ an abelian scheme over R/I. Then there is an abelian scheme A over R with A ×_{Spec R} Spec(R/I) ≅ A₀, so the deformation theory of abelian schemes over affine bases is unobstructed. The reference is F. Oort, Finite group schemes, local moduli for abelian varieties, and lifting problems, Compositio Mathematica 23, 1971, where the result is credited to Grothendieck.
differences: The Lean text assumes I² = 0, while the published theorem allows any nilpotent ideal, and the nilpotent case follows from the square-zero case by lifting along the quotients R/I^k one step at a time.
The Lean definition of an abelian scheme lists commutativity as an axiom, which for smooth proper group schemes with geometrically connected fibres follows from the other conditions.
The Lean text does not state the description of the set of lifts or the smoothness of the local moduli that accompany the published theorem.
a.why: The Lean definitions match the usual notions of abelian scheme and of base change of group schemes, but I am less certain of the exact form and source of Grothendieck's lifting theorem over arbitrary affine bases.

b.states: Take a commutative ring R with an ideal I such that I² = 0, a commutative ring R₀ with a surjective ring map π from R to R₀ whose kernel is I, and a group object A₀ in schemes over Spec R₀ that is an abelian scheme, which here means commutative, smooth, proper and with geometrically connected structure morphism. Then there are a group object A in schemes over Spec R and a morphism i from A₀ to A with three properties. The square formed by i, the two structure maps and Spec π is a pullback. The map i carries the product of any two points of A₀ over Spec R₀ to the product of the corresponding points of A. A is an abelian scheme over Spec R.
b.classical_name: Grothendieck's theorem that deformations of abelian schemes are unobstructed, so that every abelian scheme lifts along a square-zero thickening of affine schemes

differences: The Lean text assumes I² = 0, while some published versions allow any nilpotent ideal, and the nilpotent case follows from the square-zero case by lifting along the quotients R/I^(k+1) → R/I^k one step at a time.
The Lean definition of an abelian scheme lists commutativity as an axiom, which for smooth proper group schemes with geometrically connected fibres follows from the other conditions.

The Lean text expresses that A₀ is the base change of A as a group scheme by a pullback square together with the compatibility of i with the group laws on points, which is equivalent to an isomorphism A ×_{Spec R} Spec R₀ ≅ A₀ of group schemes.
The Lean text asserts only the existence of a lift and says nothing about the set of all lifts.
check.note: I judge it the same because unobstructedness is classically stated for square-zero thickenings, and the version for a nilpotent ideal, on which A bases its verdict of special case, follows from the square-zero version by lifting one step at a time, so the two forms are equivalent.

a.states: Fix a topological group G with its Borel σ-algebra, a finite index set n, a group homomorphism ι from G into the n×n complex matrices that is a closed embedding of G into GL_n(ℂ), a left Haar measure μ, a neighbourhood V of the identity and a function f in CcMat ι. The project defines CcMat ι as the space of compactly supported functions on G of the form Φ∘ι with Φ a real-smooth function on the matrix space, which for this closed linear group is the space C_c^∞(G). The text claims that there are N and functions g₁, …, g_N, h₁, …, h_N in CcMat ι such that the closed support of each g_i lies in V, the closed support of each h_i lies in the closed support of f, and f = Σ g_i * h_i with (g * h)(y) = ∫ g(x) h(x⁻¹y) dμ(x).
a.notation: G ≅ closed subgroup of GL_n(ℂ), μ left Haar measure, V ∈ 𝒩(1), f ∈ C_c^∞(G) ⇒ ∃ N, g_i, h_i ∈ C_c^∞(G) with supp g_i ⊆ V, supp h_i ⊆ supp f and f = Σ_{i=1}^N g_i * h_i
a.classical_name: Dixmier–Malliavin factorisation theorem
a.classical: For a real Lie group G, every function in C_c^∞(G) is a finite sum of convolutions g * h with g, h ∈ C_c^∞(G), and for a continuous representation of G on a Fréchet space every smooth vector is a finite sum of vectors π(g)v with g ∈ C_c^∞(G) and v smooth. The reference is J. Dixmier and P. Malliavin, Factorisations de fonctions et de vecteurs indéfiniment différentiables, Bulletin des Sciences Mathématiques 102, 1978.
differences: The Lean text covers only groups that embed as closed subgroups of GL_n(ℂ), while the published theorem covers every real Lie group, including groups with no faithful finite-dimensional representation such as the universal cover of SL₂(ℝ).

The Lean text adds that each g_i is supported in a prescribed neighbourhood V of the identity and each h_i inside the support of f, refinements that the construction in Dixmier and Malliavin's proof yields but that the theorem as usually stated does not contain.

The Lean text describes smooth functions as restrictions of smooth functions on the matrix space, which for a closed subgroup of GL_n(ℂ) gives exactly the compactly supported smooth functions on the Lie group.
The Lean text omits the version for smooth vectors of Fréchet representations.
a.why: The core factorisation is the Dixmier–Malliavin theorem, but I am not certain whether the published statement already includes the two support conditions, which decides between stronger and special case, and the Lean text is in any case narrower in its class of groups.

b.states: Take a topological group G with a Borel measurable structure, a finite index type n and a group homomorphism ι from G to the n × n complex matrices whose induced map into GL_n(ℂ) is a closed embedding. For every Haar measure μ, every neighbourhood V of the identity and every f in CcMat ι, there are N and functions g_1, …, g_N and h_1, …, h_N in CcMat ι with f = Σ_i g_i * h_i, where (g * h)(y) = ∫ g(x) h(x⁻¹y) dμ(x). Each g_i has closed support inside V, and each h_i has closed support inside the closed support of f. CcMat ι is the space of compactly supported functions on G of the form g ↦ Φ(ι(g)) with Φ infinitely differentiable over ℝ on the space of n × n complex matrices, and for such a closed linear group it is the space of compactly supported smooth functions.
b.classical_name: Dixmier–Malliavin factorisation theorem, that every compactly supported smooth function on a Lie group is a finite sum of convolutions of two such functions (Dixmier and Malliavin 1978)
differences: The Lean text covers only groups that embed as closed subgroups of GL_n(ℂ), the linear Lie groups. The published theorem holds for every Lie group, including nonlinear ones such as the universal cover of SL_2(ℝ).

Smoothness on G is expressed as being the restriction of a smooth function on the ambient matrix space. For compactly supported functions on a closed subgroup this agrees with smoothness on the Lie group.

The Lean text adds that each h_i is supported inside the support of f. The bare published statement does not mention this refinement, but the standard proof gives it, because the h_i arise from f through differential operators.

The Lean text covers only groups with a closed embedding into GL_n(ℂ), while the published theorem covers every Lie group, including groups with no faithful finite-dimensional representation such as the universal cover of SL₂(ℝ).

The Lean text describes the smooth functions on G as the compactly supported functions of the form Φ∘ι with Φ real-smooth on the matrix space, which for a closed subgroup of GL_n(ℂ) gives exactly the compactly supported smooth functions on the Lie group.

a.states: For every non-archimedean local field k with its valuation topology, every natural number n and every complex vector space V carrying a representation π of the group GL_n(k), the text assumes that π is smooth and irreducible. Smooth means that the stabilizer of every vector of V is an open subset of GL_n(k), where GL_n(k) carries the topology that Mathlib gives to units of the matrix ring, which is the usual topology from the matrix entries. Irreducible is Mathlib's algebraic notion, so V is nonzero and has no invariant subspaces other than 0 and V. The conclusion is that π is admissible, which the project defines as smooth together with the condition that for every compact open subgroup K of GL_n(k) the space of K-fixed vectors is finite-dimensional over ℂ.

a.classical: Every irreducible smooth complex representation of GL_n(F), for F a non-archimedean local field, is admissible, and Bernstein extended the result to every reductive group over F. Reference I. N. Bernstein and A. V. Zelevinsky, Representations of the group GL(n,F) where F is a local non-archimedean field, Russian Mathematical Surveys 31, 1976.

a.classical_name: Existence of the metaplectic representation (Segal, Shale, Weil)
a.classical: The real symplectic group Sp(2n,ℝ) has a connected double cover Mp(2n,ℝ) that carries a unique strongly continuous unitary representation μ on L²(ℝⁿ) with μ(g)ρ(w)μ(g)⁻¹ = ρ(gw) for the Schrödinger representation ρ of the Heisenberg group, and μ does not factor through Sp(2n,ℝ). The operators μ(g) preserve the Schwartz space, the inverse image of the maximal compact subgroup U(n) acts on the Gaussian by a square root of the inverse determinant, and the Gaussian matrix coefficient is a square root of det P(g)⁻¹ up to the normalization of the Gaussian. Reference G. B. Folland, Harmonic Analysis in Phase Space, Annals of Mathematics Studies 122, 1989, Chapter 4.

The Lean text does not state that G is connected, although its kernel clause together with ω(z) = −1 rules out the trivial double cover Sp(2n,ℝ) × ℤ/2.

The Lean text adds joint continuity of (g, φ) ↦ ω(g)φ in the Fréchet topology of the Schwartz space, which follows from the identification of 𝓢 with the smooth vectors of the representation but is not part of the usual statement.

a.states: For every totally real number field F, every nonzero ideal 𝔣 of its ring of integers and every rational-valued function ε on ideals that takes equal values on ideals coprime to 𝔣 in the same narrow ray class modulo 𝔣, the text asserts that some function L on ℂ has two properties. Moreover L(1 − k) is a rational number for every integer k ≥ 1. Two ideals I and J coprime to 𝔣 lie in the same narrow ray class when (a)I = (b)J for nonzero totally positive integers a, b with a ≡ b ≡ 1 mod 𝔣.

a.classical_name: Siegel–Klingen theorem
a.classical: For a totally real number field F, a nonzero integral ideal 𝔣 and a narrow ray class C modulo 𝔣, the partial zeta function ζ(C, s), the sum of N(I)^{−s} over the integral ideals I in C, continues meromorphically to ℂ with at most a simple pole at s = 1, and ζ(C, 1 − k) is rational for every integer k ≥ 1. Klingen proved the case of the Dedekind zeta function in 1962 and Siegel the case of partial zeta functions. Reference C. L. Siegel, Über die Fourierschen Koeffizienten von Modulformen, Nachrichten der Akademie der Wissenschaften in Göttingen, 1970.
differences: The Lean text treats any rational-valued function on narrow ray classes instead of a single class, which is equivalent because such a function is a rational linear combination of class indicators.

The Lean text asks only for a function holomorphic away from s = 1 and leaves the value at 1 and the kind of singularity unspecified, which does not affect the values at 1 − k because the continuation is unique on the connected set ℂ ∖ {1}.
a.vacuity: None found, since constant functions satisfy the ray hypothesis and the uniqueness of the continuation gives the rationality claim real content.
a.why: The ray relation, the coprimality condition and the Dirichlet series in the dossier match the standard narrow ray class partial zeta functions, and uniqueness of continuation makes the existential form equivalent to the published one.

Moreover, L(1 − k) is a rational number for every natural number k ≥ 1. The Lean text treats every ℚ-valued function ε that is constant on the narrow ray classes of ideals coprime to 𝔣 in place of a single partial zeta function, which is equivalent because the indicator of one class is such an ε and the values are linear in ε.

H is a finite abelian extension of K in which every nonzero prime is unramified and contains every other such extension inside ℂ, and art sends the class of every nonzero prime 𝔭 to an arithmetic Frobenius element at every prime of H above 𝔭. For every invertible fractional ideal 𝔞 and every lattice L in ℂ equal to the image of 𝔞, the field K(j(L)) equals H, where j(L) = 1728 g₂³/(g₂³ − 27g₃²) is the j-invariant of the curve y² = x³ − (g₂/4)x − g₃/4. For all fractional ideals 𝔞 and 𝔟 and lattices L and L′ equal to the images of 𝔞 and 𝔟⁻¹𝔞, the automorphism art([𝔟]) sends j(L) to j(L′).

a.states: For every field k of characteristic zero, all natural numbers N and D, and every homogeneous ideal I of k[x_0, …, x_{N−1}] whose extension to k̄[x] is prime and for which k[x]/I has Krull dimension D + 1, the text asserts that a Chow form of I exists and is unique up to a nonzero factor in k. A Chow form here is a polynomial f over k in D + 1 blocks of N variables u_{i,j} that is homogeneous of degree d in each block, is irreducible over k̄, and vanishes at u ∈ k̄^{(D+1)×N} exactly when some nonzero point y of the zero set of I in k̄^N satisfies Σ_j u_{i,j}y_j = 0 for every i. The degree d is the floor of (deg P)! times the leading coefficient of the Hilbert polynomial P of k[x]/I, which is the degree of the projective variety V(I) of dimension D. Uniqueness means that every polynomial with these three properties equals cf for some nonzero c ∈ k.
a.notation: ∀ k with char k = 0, ∀ I ⊂ k[x_0..x_{N−1}] homogeneous with I·k̄[x] prime and dim k[x]/I = D + 1, ∃! up to k^× f ∈ k[u_{i,j}] (i ≤ D, j < N) multihomogeneous of degree deg V(I) in each u_i, irreducible over k̄, with f(u) = 0 ⇔ ∃ y ∈ V(I)(k̄) ∖ {0}, u_i·y = 0 for all i
a.classical_name: Existence and uniqueness of the Chow form (Cayley, Chow and van der Waerden)
a.classical: For an irreducible projective variety X ⊂ ℙ^{N−1} of dimension D and degree d, the (D + 1)-tuples of hyperplanes that meet X form an irreducible hypersurface in the product of dual spaces, cut out by an irreducible form that is multihomogeneous of degree d in each block and unique up to a scalar. When X is defined over a field k, the form can be taken with coefficients in k. Reference W.-L. Chow and B. L. van der Waerden, Zur algebraischen Geometrie IX. Über zugeordnete Formen und algebraische Systeme von algebraischen Mannigfaltigkeiten, Mathematische Annalen 113, 1937.
differences: The Lean text assumes characteristic zero, while the published theorem holds over every field.
The Lean text treats only varieties defined over k that stay irreducible over k̄, and it includes the descent of the form to coefficients in k among its conclusions.
The Lean text defines the degree through the Hilbert polynomial of k[x]/I, which agrees with the usual degree of the variety.
a.vacuity: None found, since for N ≥ 1 the zero ideal with D = N − 1 meets every hypothesis and the determinant of the N × N matrix (u_{i,j}) is then its Chow form.
a.why: The three defining clauses are the textbook characterization of the Chow form, and the Hilbert-polynomial normalization gives the usual degree.

a.states: For every field k of characteristic zero, all natural numbers N and e, and every homogeneous prime ideal P of k[x_0, …, x_{N−1}] for which k[x]/P has Krull dimension e + 1, the text asserts that there is a polynomial f over k, unique up to a nonzero factor in k, with three properties. The polynomial f in e + 1 blocks of N variables is homogeneous of degree d in each block, where d is the floor of (deg Q)! times the leading coefficient of the Hilbert polynomial Q of k[x]/P. It is irreducible in k[u], and it vanishes at u ∈ k̄^{(e+1)×N} exactly when some nonzero point of the zero set of P in k̄^N lies on all e + 1 hyperplanes u_i. The ideal P need not stay prime after extension to k̄, so its zero set over k̄ may consist of several Galois-conjugate components.

Over k̄ this form is the product of the Chow forms of the conjugate components of that zero set. Reference Yu. V. Nesterenko and P. Philippon (editors), Introduction to Algebraic Independence Theory, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1752, 2001.

a.states: For every field K of characteristic zero and every linearly ordered set A, the text considers the shuffle algebra over K on the alphabet A, which is the vector space with basis all finite words over A, with the shuffle product and the empty word as unit, and the polynomial ring over K with one variable for each Lyndon word. A Lyndon word is a nonempty word that is strictly smaller in the lexicographic order than each of its proper nonempty suffixes. The text asserts that the K-algebra homomorphism sending the variable of each Lyndon word w to the word w itself is bijective.

A Lyndon word is a nonempty word that is lexicographically smaller than each of its proper nonempty suffixes. The shuffle algebra is the space of finitely supported K-linear combinations of words with the recursively defined shuffle product and the empty word as unit.
b.classical_name: Radford's theorem that the shuffle algebra over a field of characteristic zero is the polynomial algebra on the Lyndon words

a.states: For every field k of characteristic zero and every reduced scheme X with a morphism g to Spec k that is locally of finite type, quasi-compact and separated, the statement asserts that there are a scheme X' and a morphism s from X' to X with four properties. The morphism s is a finite composite of blowups, each defined by the universal property of blowing up an arbitrary quasi-coherent ideal sheaf on the previous scheme, with no condition on the centres. The composite of s with g is smooth, so X' is smooth over k, and s restricts to an isomorphism over the open locus where g is smooth. The reduced ideal sheaf of the preimage under s of the non-smooth locus of g is a strict normal crossings divisor, in the sense that near every point of X' it is generated on an affine neighbourhood by a product of some members of one regular system of parameters at that point.
a.notation: ∀ k with char k = 0, ∀ X reduced, separated and of finite type over k, ∃ s = π_1 ∘ ⋯ ∘ π_r from X' to X with each π_j a blowup along some ideal sheaf, X' smooth over k, s an isomorphism over X_sm, and (s^{-1}(X ∖ X_sm))_red an snc divisor
a.classical_name: Hironaka's resolution of singularities in its strong form

Then there is a finite sequence of blowups X' = X_r → ⋯ → X_0 = X along smooth centres lying over the singular locus such that X' is smooth, the composite is an isomorphism over the smooth locus of X, and the preimage of the singular locus is a divisor with simple normal crossings. Reference is H. Hironaka, Resolution of singularities of an algebraic variety over a field of characteristic zero I, II, Annals of Mathematics 79, 1964.

a.why: Every clause of the Lean conclusion is a clause of the strong resolution theorem once the project's blowup and snc definitions are unwound, and the only change is that the smoothness of the centres is dropped.

a.states: For every number field K and every nonzero ideal 𝔮 of its ring of integers, the statement asserts that there is a finite abelian Galois extension L of K with three properties. Every prime of K that does not divide 𝔮 is unramified in L, which the project expresses by saying that every Galois element acting trivially modulo some prime above it is the identity. The Frobenius elements at the primes not dividing 𝔮 generate Gal(L/K). For every nonzero integral ideal I coprime to 𝔮, every character of Gal(L/K) takes the value 1 on the Artin symbol of I exactly when I·(β) = (α) for nonzero integers α and β of K that are coprime to 𝔮, satisfy α ≡ β mod 𝔮 and have a quotient α/β that is positive at every real embedding.
a.notation: ∀ K, ∀ 𝔮 ≠ 0, ∃ L/K finite abelian with 𝔭 unramified for all 𝔭 ∤ 𝔮, ⟨Frob_𝔭 | 𝔭 ∤ 𝔮⟩ = Gal(L/K), and for every integral I ≠ 0 prime to 𝔮, Art_{L/K}(I) = 1 ⟺ I = (α/β) with α, β ∈ O_K prime to 𝔮, α ≡ β mod 𝔮, α/β ≫ 0
a.classical_name: Existence theorem for ray class fields (Takagi)
a.classical: For every modulus 𝔪 of a number field K, made of a nonzero integral ideal and a set of real places, there is an abelian extension K_𝔪 of K that is unramified outside 𝔪 and for which the Artin map induces an isomorphism from the ray class group I^𝔪/P_{𝔪,1} onto Gal(K_𝔪/K). Reference is J. Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, 1999, Chapter VI, Section 6.
differences: The Lean statement treats only moduli whose infinite part contains every real place, because its ray condition asks α/β to be positive at all real embeddings, while the published theorem allows any set of real places in the modulus.
a.why: Unwinding the definitions shows that the third clause identifies the kernel of the Artin map on ideals prime to 𝔮 with the narrow ray group modulo 𝔮, which together with the first two clauses is the defining property of the ray class field for the modulus 𝔮 times all real places.

b.states: For every number field K and every nonzero ideal 𝔮 of its ring of integers, the Lean text asserts that there is a number field L that is an abelian Galois extension of K with three properties. Every prime of K that does not divide 𝔮 is unramified in L, and the Frobenius elements of these primes generate the Galois group of L over K. For every nonzero ideal I coprime to 𝔮, every character of the Galois group with values in the nonzero complex numbers sends I to 1, through the product of its values on the Frobenius elements of the prime factors of I, exactly when I times (β) equals (α) for nonzero integers α and β that are prime to 𝔮, congruent modulo 𝔮 and of positive product under every real embedding. Together these properties say that the Artin map identifies the ray class group modulo 𝔮 times all real places with the Galois group of L over K.
b.classical_name: Existence theorem of class field theory for ray class fields (Takagi, Artin)

a.states: For every scheme S, every group scheme G over S and every S-scheme X with an action of G, the statement assumes that G is finite, flat and locally of finite presentation over S, that G(T) acts freely on X(T) for every S-scheme T, and that the set-theoretic orbit of every point of X lies in an affine open subscheme. It concludes that there are an S-scheme Y and a G-invariant S-morphism q from X to Y such that the induced map from the presheaf T ↦ X(T)/G(T) to the functor of points of Y is locally injective and locally surjective for the fppf topology over S, so Y represents the fppf quotient sheaf. It also concludes that q is an fppf G-torsor, which here means that the map from G ×_S X to X ×_Y X given by the action and the projection is an isomorphism and that q has sections over some jointly surjective family of flat morphisms of finite presentation into Y.

a.classical_name: Quotient of a scheme by a finite locally free group scheme (SGA 3, Exposé V, Théorème 4.1)
a.classical: Let G be a finite locally free group scheme over S acting on an S-scheme X such that the orbit of every point lies in an affine open subset. Then the quotient Y = X/G exists as a scheme and as a quotient in ringed spaces, and the map from X to Y is integral, surjective and G-invariant. If G acts freely, the map from X to Y is finite locally free, the map from G ×_S X to X ×_Y X is an isomorphism, X is a G-torsor over Y, and Y represents the fppf quotient sheaf. Reference is M. Demazure and A. Grothendieck, Schémas en groupes I (SGA 3), Lecture Notes in Mathematics 151, 1970.

The Lean conclusion keeps only the fppf quotient property and the torsor property and omits that q is finite, locally free and surjective and that Y is also the quotient in the category of ringed spaces.

It also concludes that the square formed by the action map and the second projection from G times X to X, with q on both remaining sides, is cartesian, and that q has sections over a jointly surjective family of flat morphisms locally of finite presentation, so q is an fppf G-torsor.

a.states: For every discrete valuation ring R with finite residue field and fraction field K, and every abelian scheme A over Spec K, meaning a commutative group scheme that is smooth, proper and geometrically connected, the statement considers any number field F. It assumes that A has some relative dimension d with the degree of F over ℚ equal to 2d, and that some domain O with fraction field F acts on A through a ring homomorphism into the endomorphisms of A defined over K. The homomorphism is not required to be injective, but it is injective automatically because a nonzero kernel would contain a nonzero integer, so the hypothesis is the usual condition that F embeds in the endomorphism algebra of A. It concludes that A has potential good reduction with respect to R, meaning that there are a finite extension L of K and a discrete valuation ring W with fraction field L and W ∩ K = R such that A ×_K L is the generic fibre of an abelian scheme over W, by an isomorphism that respects the group law.
