a.classical_name: Serre–Tate theorem on potential good reduction of abelian varieties with complex multiplication
a.classical: Let K be a field with a discrete valuation and A an abelian variety over K with complex multiplication over K, so that End_K(A) ⊗ ℚ contains a commutative semisimple subalgebra of degree 2 dim A. Then A has potential good reduction, so it acquires good reduction over a finite extension of K. Reference is J.-P. Serre and J. Tate, Good reduction of abelian varieties, Annals of Mathematics 88, 1968.
differences: The Lean statement requires the residue field of R to be finite, while the published theorem allows any discrete valuation.

The Lean statement requires the complex multiplication to come from a single number field F of degree 2 dim A, while the published theorem allows a commutative semisimple algebra of that degree, which can be a product of fields.
a.why: The project's definitions of abelian scheme, complex multiplication and potential good reduction match the standard notions, and the only changes are the finite residue field and the requirement that the CM algebra be a field.

b.states: For every discrete valuation ring R with finite residue field and fraction field K, and every abelian variety A over K, given as a commutative group object over Spec K that is smooth, proper and geometrically connected, the Lean text takes every number field F. If A is smooth of some relative dimension d, the degree of F over ℚ equals 2d, and some ring O with fraction field F acts on A by K-endomorphisms through a ring homomorphism, then A has potential good reduction. Potential good reduction means that there are a finite extension L of K and a discrete valuation ring W with fraction field L and W ∩ K = R such that the base change of A to L is isomorphic, as a group object, to the generic fibre of an abelian scheme over W.
b.classical_name: Serre–Tate theorem that an abelian variety with complex multiplication has potential good reduction
differences: The Lean statement requires the residue field of R to be finite, while Serre and Tate prove the result for an arbitrary discrete valuation.
The Lean statement requires the complex multiplication to come from a single number field of degree 2 dim A, while the published theorem allows a commutative semisimple algebra of that degree.

The Lean statement requires the endomorphisms to be defined over K, while the published result also covers complex multiplication defined only over an algebraic closure by first passing to a finite extension.

The Lean action of O is not required to be injective, but injectivity follows because the endomorphism ring of a nonzero abelian variety is torsion-free, so the hypothesis still expresses complex multiplication.
The Lean statement requires the residue field of R to be finite, while Serre and Tate prove the result for an arbitrary discrete valuation.

The Lean statement requires the complex multiplication to come from one number field F of degree 2d over ℚ, while the published theorem allows a commutative semisimple algebra of that degree, which can be a product of fields.

The Lean statement requires OAct to act by endomorphisms of A over Spec K, which matches the published theorem for complex multiplication over K but leaves out its corollary for complex multiplication that is defined only over an algebraic closure.

The Lean statement does not require the map from O to the endomorphisms of A to be injective, but a nonzero kernel would contain a nonzero integer m, and multiplication by m is a nonzero endomorphism because d is at least 1, so the hypothesis still expresses complex multiplication by F.

a.states: Let k be a field of characteristic zero, P a homogeneous prime ideal of k[x_0, …, x_{N−1}] with Krull dimension of k[x]/P equal to e + 2, so that V(P) is a projective variety of dimension e + 1, and u ∈ k^N a vector whose linear form ℓ_u = Σ u_j x_j does not lie in P. Suppose that f, a polynomial in e + 2 blocks of N variables, is a Chow form of P in the project's sense, namely an irreducible polynomial over k, homogeneous of one common degree in each block, whose zeros over the algebraic closure are exactly the tuples of e + 2 linear forms that have a common nonzero zero on V(P). Suppose also that for every prime Q in the hyperplane-section cycle of P + (ℓ_u), whose members are the minimal primes other than the irrelevant ideal with multiplicity m_Q equal to the length of the localisation at Q, the polynomial g_Q in e + 1 blocks is a Chow form of Q in the same sense. Then substituting u for the first block of variables in f gives c·∏_Q g_Q^{m_Q} for some nonzero constant c in k.
a.notation: char k = 0, P homogeneous prime, dim k[x]/P = e + 2, ℓ_u ∉ P, f = Ch_P, g_Q = Ch_Q for V(P)·H_u = Σ m_Q [Q] with m_Q = length(k[x]_Q/(P + (ℓ_u))) ⟹ ∃ c ∈ k^×, f(u, U_1, …, U_{e+1}) = c ∏_Q g_Q(U_1, …, U_{e+1})^{m_Q}
a.classical_name: Chow form of a hyperplane section
a.classical: If V is an irreducible projective variety of dimension r ≥ 1 with Chow form Ch_V and H_u is a hyperplane that does not contain V, then the Chow form of the intersection cycle V·H_u, the product of the Chow forms of its components raised to their intersection multiplicities, equals Ch_V(u, U_1, …, U_r) up to a nonzero constant factor. Reference is P. Philippon, Critères pour l'indépendance algébrique, Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS 64, 1986.
differences: The Lean statement restricts the ground field to characteristic zero, while the published identity is stated without that restriction for Chow forms of cycles.
a.why: The project's Chow form agrees with the usual one up to a constant because a prime ideal stays radical over the algebraic closure in characteristic zero, and its length multiplicities are the intersection multiplicities with a Cartier divisor, but the identity is a folklore lemma of elimination theory whose exact published wording and field hypotheses vary between sources.

b.states: For every field k of characteristic zero, all natural numbers N and e, and every homogeneous prime ideal P of k[x_0,…,x_{N−1}] whose quotient ring has Krull dimension e+2, the Lean text takes a vector u in k^N whose linear form ℓ_u = Σ u_j x_j is not in P. It takes an irreducible polynomial f in e+2 blocks of N variables, of one common degree in each block, whose zeros over the algebraic closure are exactly the tuples of e+2 hyperplanes that meet the zero set of P in a common nonzero point, so f is a Chow form of P. It also takes, for every minimal prime Q of P + (ℓ_u) other than an irrelevant one, a Chow form g(Q) of Q of the same kind in e+1 blocks. It concludes that substituting u into the first block of f gives a nonzero constant times the product of the g(Q), each raised to the length of the localisation at Q of the quotient by P + (ℓ_u).
b.classical_name: Specialisation formula for the Chow form of a hyperplane section, which gives the Chow form of the cycle V·H from the Chow form of V (Nesterenko, Philippon)
differences: The Lean statement is restricted to fields of characteristic zero, while the classical formula holds over any field when Chow forms of cycles are used.

The Lean statement treats an irreducible variety given by a prime ideal and always specialises the first block, while the published formula is usually stated for cycles and any block and reduces to this case by multiplicativity and the symmetry of the Chow form.

The Lean statement is restricted to fields of characteristic zero, where an irreducible polynomial with the zero set that IsChowFormInt requires is the Chow form up to a nonzero constant, while the published identity holds over any field when Chow forms of cycles are used.

The Lean statement treats one variety given by a homogeneous prime ideal and specialises only the first block of f, and the published versions for cycles and for other blocks reduce to this case by multiplicativity and the symmetry of the Chow form.

a.states: Let F be a totally real number field, l a prime and n ≥ 1, and let ε be a rational-valued function on ideals of the ring of integers that is constant on narrow ray classes modulo l^n among nonzero ideals coprime to l and that takes l-integral values on those ideals. Let 𝔠 be a nonzero ideal coprime to l and k ≥ 1 an integer. Suppose r is the value at 1 − k of a function holomorphic on ℂ ∖ {1} that equals the Dirichlet series Σ ε(I) N(I)^{−s} over nonzero ideals I coprime to l for Re s > 1, and r' is the corresponding value for the translated function I ↦ ε(𝔠I). Then r − N(𝔠)^k r' is l-integral, that is, it lies in ℤ_(l).
a.notation: F totally real, ε constant on Cl^+_F(l^n) with values in ℤ_(l), (𝔠, l) = 1, k ≥ 1 ⟹ ζ(ε, 1 − k) − N𝔠^k ζ(ε_𝔠, 1 − k) ∈ ℤ_(l), where ζ(ε, s) = Σ_{(I, l) = 1} ε(I) N I^{−s} and ε_𝔠(I) = ε(𝔠I)
a.classical_name: Deligne–Ribet integrality theorem for partial zeta values of totally real fields
a.classical: Let F be totally real, 𝔣 an integral ideal, p a prime and ε a locally constant ℤ_p-valued function on the narrow ray class group of F modulo 𝔣p^∞. For an integral ideal 𝔠 prime to 𝔣p and an integer k ≥ 1, the smoothed value ζ(ε, 1 − k) − N𝔠^k ζ(ε_𝔠, 1 − k), with ε_𝔠(𝔞) = ε(𝔠𝔞) and partial zeta functions summed over ideals prime to 𝔣p, lies in ℤ_p. Reference is P. Deligne and K. A. Ribet, Values of abelian L-functions at negative integers over totally real fields, Inventiones Mathematicae 59, 1980.
differences: The Lean statement takes the modulus to be a power of l alone, while the published theorem allows an arbitrary auxiliary ideal 𝔣 next to the powers of p.

The Lean statement uses rational-valued functions with l-integral values, while the published theorem allows ℤ_p-valued functions, although the two forms of the integrality claim are equivalent by linearity.
a.why: The hypotheses and the smoothed combination match the Deligne–Ribet integrality statement, and a check over ℚ at k = 1 with Hurwitz zeta values confirms the direction of the translation ε(𝔠I), but the paper's exact normalisation is recalled from memory.

b.states: For every totally real number field F, every prime l and every n ≥ 1, the Lean text takes a rational-valued function ε on ideals that is constant on narrow ray classes modulo l^n and l-integral on every ideal coprime to l. For every ideal 𝔠 coprime to l, every k ≥ 1 and all rationals r and r', it assumes that r is the value at 1−k of a function holomorphic on ℂ∖{1} that equals the partial zeta series Σ ε(I) N(I)^(−s) over ideals I coprime to l for Re s > 1, and that r' is the same value for the translated function I ↦ ε(𝔠I). It concludes that r − N(𝔠)^k r' is l-integral.
b.classical_name: Deligne–Ribet congruences for partial zeta values of totally real fields, the integrality of Δ_𝔠 ζ(ε, 1−k)
differences: The Lean statement uses only moduli that are powers of l, so the auxiliary conductor 𝔣 prime to l in the work of Deligne and Ribet is the unit ideal.

The Lean statement takes ε rational-valued and constant on classes modulo one fixed l^n, while Deligne and Ribet allow every locally constant ℤ_l-valued function on the narrow ray class group modulo 𝔣l^∞.
The Lean statement leaves out the l-adic measure and the l-adic L-function that Deligne and Ribet construct from these congruences.
The Lean statement uses only the moduli powMod F l n, which are powers of l, so the auxiliary ideal 𝔣 of Deligne and Ribet is the unit ideal.

The Lean statement takes ε rational-valued, l-integral on ideals coprime to l and constant on narrow ray classes modulo one fixed l^n, while Deligne and Ribet take a locally constant ℤ_l-valued function on the narrow ray class group modulo 𝔣l^∞, and for 𝔣 equal to the unit ideal the two forms are equivalent by linearity in ε.

a.states: Let K be a number field, L and L' finite abelian Galois extensions of K, and 𝔪 a nonzero ideal of the ring of integers of K. Assume that L satisfies the project's ray class field condition for 𝔪, the same three clauses as the field in proposition 32, which make L the ray class field of K for the modulus 𝔪 times all real places. Assume also that every character χ of Gal(L'/K) is unramified at every prime not dividing 𝔪 and takes equal values on the Artin symbols of (α) and (β) whenever α and β are nonzero integers coprime to 𝔪 with α ≡ β mod 𝔪 and α/β positive at every real embedding. Then L' admits a K-algebra embedding into L.
a.notation: L = K_{𝔪∞} the narrow ray class field mod 𝔪, L'/K abelian, every χ of Gal(L'/K) unramified outside 𝔪 with χ(Art(α)) = χ(Art(β)) whenever α ≡ β mod 𝔪 and α/β ≫ 0 ⟹ ∃ a K-embedding L' ↪ L
a.classical_name: Maximality of the ray class field in class field theory
a.classical: The ray class field K_𝔪 of a number field K for a modulus 𝔪 contains every abelian extension L'/K whose conductor divides 𝔪, equivalently every abelian extension unramified outside 𝔪 whose Artin map kills the ray P_{𝔪,1}. Reference is J. Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, 1999, Chapter VI, Section 6.
differences: The Lean statement treats only moduli whose infinite part contains every real place, while the published theorem allows any set of real places in the modulus.
a.why: Taking β = 1 in the character condition shows that the Artin map of L' kills every principal ideal with a totally positive generator congruent to 1 mod 𝔪, which is the condition that the conductor of L' divides 𝔪 times all real places, and the conclusion is the standard containment of L' in the ray class field.

b.states: For all number fields K, L and L' with L and L' abelian Galois over K, and every nonzero ideal 𝔪 of the ring of integers of K, the Lean text assumes that L is unramified at the primes not dividing 𝔪, is generated by their Frobenius elements, and has as Artin kernel on ideals prime to 𝔪 exactly the narrow ray modulo 𝔪, so L is the narrow ray class field of 𝔪. It further assumes that every character χ of the Galois group of L' over K is unramified at every prime not dividing 𝔪 and takes equal values on (α) and (β) whenever α and β are nonzero, prime to 𝔪, congruent modulo 𝔪 and of positive product under every real embedding. It concludes that there is a K-algebra embedding of L' into L.
b.classical_name: Characterisation of the ray class field as the largest abelian extension whose conductor divides the modulus (class field theory)
differences: The Lean statement fixes the infinite part of the modulus to be all real places, so it covers only narrow ray class fields.

The Lean statement expresses the condition that the conductor of L' divides the modulus through the characters of its Galois group, which is equivalent to the usual conductor condition by Artin reciprocity.
The Lean conclusion is an abstract K-embedding of L' into L in place of an inclusion of subfields of a fixed algebraic closure.
The Lean statement takes L to be the ray class field for 𝔪 times all real places, because RayPair asks for positivity at every real embedding, so it covers only narrow ray class fields.

The Lean statement expresses the condition that the conductor of L' divides 𝔪 times all real places through IsModulus for every character of the Galois group of L' over K, and taking β = 1 in RayPair shows that this is equivalent to the usual conductor condition.
The Lean conclusion is a K-algebra embedding of L' into L, which is equivalent to the inclusion of L' in L inside a fixed algebraic closure.

a.states: Let K be an imaginary quadratic field with a chosen embedding into ℂ and discriminant less than −4, so that its only units are ±1. Let Λ be a period lattice whose points are exactly the images of the integers of K, with Weierstrass invariants g₂ and g₃ and Weierstrass function ℘, and let n be a positive integer. The statement asserts that the field generated over K by g₂³/(g₂³ − 27g₃²) and by the numbers g₂g₃/(g₂³ − 27g₃²)·℘(z/n) for z ∈ Λ with z/n ∉ Λ is a number field, is abelian Galois over K, and satisfies the project's ray class field condition for the ideal nO_K. Because K has no real embeddings, that condition says that this field is the ray class field of K modulo n, and the generators are j/1728 and a constant multiple of the Weber function at the nonzero n-torsion points.
a.notation: K imaginary quadratic, d_K < −4, Λ = O_K ⊂ ℂ, n ≥ 1 ⟹ K(g₂³/Δ, g₂g₃Δ^{−1}℘(z/n) for z ∈ Λ ∖ nΛ) is the ray class field of K modulo nO_K, with Δ = g₂³ − 27g₃²
a.classical_name: Weber–Hasse theorem on ray class fields of imaginary quadratic fields (main theorem of complex multiplication)
a.classical: Let K be an imaginary quadratic field, E an elliptic curve over ℂ with End(E) ≅ O_K, h a Weber function for E and 𝔠 a nonzero integral ideal of O_K. Then K(j(E), h(E[𝔠])) is the ray class field of K modulo 𝔠. Reference is J. H. Silverman, Advanced Topics in the Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, 1994, Chapter II, Theorem 5.6.
differences: The Lean statement excludes the fields ℚ(i) and ℚ(√−3), whose discriminants are −4 and −3, while the published theorem covers every imaginary quadratic field with a Weber function adapted to the larger unit group.
The Lean statement uses only the lattice O_K itself, while the published theorem allows any elliptic curve with complex multiplication by O_K, whose lattice can lie in any ideal class.
The Lean statement uses only moduli generated by a positive integer n, while the published theorem allows every nonzero integral ideal 𝔠.
a.why: For a field without real embeddings the project's ray class field condition is the usual characterisation of the ray class field, and the adjoined numbers generate the same field over K as j(E) and the Weber function values on E[n].

b.states: For every imaginary quadratic field K of discriminant less than −4, embedded in ℂ by a given algebra map, and every period lattice in ℂ that equals the image of the ring of integers of K, the Lean text takes every n > 0. It forms the subfield of ℂ generated over K by g₂³/Δ, which equals j/1728, and by the values (g₂g₃/Δ)·℘(z/n) for lattice points z with z/n outside the lattice, where Δ = g₂³ − 27g₃². It asserts that this field is a number field, is abelian Galois over K, and is the ray class field of K modulo nO_K in the sense that it is unramified at primes not dividing n, is generated by Frobenius elements, and has the ray modulo n as Artin kernel.
b.classical_name: Weber–Hasse theorem that the ray class field of an imaginary quadratic field is generated by j and the Weber function of torsion points (main theorem of complex multiplication)
differences: The Lean statement treats only moduli generated by a positive integer n, while the published theorem covers every nonzero integral ideal 𝔠 of O_K through the 𝔠-torsion points.
The Lean statement excludes the fields of discriminant −3 and −4, where the published theorem uses a Weber function built from ℘³ or ℘².
The Lean statement fixes the lattice to be O_K itself, while the published theorem allows any elliptic curve with complex multiplication by O_K, whose lattice is homothetic to any fractional ideal.
The Lean statement treats only the moduli nO_K generated by a positive integer n, while the published theorem covers every nonzero integral ideal 𝔠 of O_K through the 𝔠-torsion points.
The Lean statement excludes the fields of discriminant −3 and −4, which the published theorem covers with a Weber function built from ℘³ or ℘².
The Lean statement fixes the lattice to be the image of O_K, while the published theorem allows any elliptic curve with complex multiplication by O_K, whose lattice can lie in any ideal class.

a.states: For every commutative ring R and natural number s, the statement assumes that every unimodular row of length m + 1 with m ≥ s can be shortened, meaning that adding suitable multiples of its last entry to the other entries gives a unimodular row of length m, which is the condition that the stable rank of R is at most s. For all natural numbers i and n with 2i + s + 2 ≤ n, it concludes that the map H_i(GL_n(R), ℤ) → H_i(GL_{n+1}(R), ℤ) on group homology with trivial integer coefficients, induced by A ↦ diag(A, 1), is an isomorphism.
a.notation: sr(R) ≤ s, n ≥ 2i + s + 2 ⟹ H_i(GL_n(R), ℤ) → H_i(GL_{n+1}(R), ℤ) is an isomorphism
a.classical_name: Homological stability for general linear groups (van der Kallen)
a.classical: Let R be a ring of finite stable rank sr(R), normalised so that fields have stable rank 1. Then the stabilisation map H_i(GL_n(R), ℤ) → H_i(GL_{n+1}(R), ℤ) is surjective for n ≥ 2i + sr(R) − 1 and an isomorphism for n ≥ 2i + sr(R). Reference is W. van der Kallen, Homology stability for linear groups, Inventiones Mathematicae 60, 1980.
differences: The Lean statement asks for n ≥ 2i + s + 2, two more than the bound n ≥ 2i + s of the published theorem, so it claims the isomorphism on a smaller range.
The Lean statement omits the surjectivity of the stabilisation map in the range n ≥ 2i + s − 1.
The Lean statement is restricted to commutative rings, while the published theorem holds for associative rings of finite stable rank.
a.vacuity: The hypothesis with s = 0 holds only for the zero ring, where every group involved is trivial, and no other emptiness was found.
a.why: The project's stable range condition is the standard one and the Lean range lies inside the isomorphism range of van der Kallen's theorem and also inside the slightly smaller range of later proofs such as that of Randal-Williams and Wahl.

b.states: For every commutative ring R and natural number s such that every unimodular row of length n+1 with n ≥ s can be shortened to a unimodular row of length n by adding multiples of its last entry, which says that the Bass stable rank of R is at most s, the Lean text takes all natural numbers i and n with 2i + s + 2 ≤ n. It asserts that the map from H_i(GL_n(R), ℤ) to H_i(GL_{n+1}(R), ℤ) with trivial integer coefficients, induced by the block inclusion that sends A to diag(A, 1), is an isomorphism.
b.classical_name: Van der Kallen's homological stability theorem for general linear groups
differences: The Lean statement demands n ≥ 2i + s + 2, while van der Kallen proves the isomorphism already for n ≥ 2i + s, so the Lean range starts two steps later.
The Lean statement is restricted to commutative rings, while van der Kallen's theorem holds for associative rings with unit.
The Lean statement leaves out the surjectivity of the map one step below the range of isomorphism.
The Lean statement asks for n ≥ 2i + s + 2, while van der Kallen proves the isomorphism for n ≥ 2i + s, so the Lean range starts two steps later.
The Lean statement is restricted to commutative rings, while van der Kallen's theorem holds for associative rings with unit.
The Lean statement leaves out the surjectivity of the stabilisation map for n ≥ 2i + s − 1.

a.states: Let k be a field of characteristic zero and X a scheme that is smooth of constant relative dimension d, quasi-compact and separated over k. Let I be an ideal sheaf on X whose zero locus contains no irreducible component of X, and let E be a closed subset of X whose reduced ideal is a simple normal crossings divisor at every point of E. The statement asserts a finite sequence of blowups s from X' to X in which every centre Z is smooth over k and has simple normal crossings with the accumulated boundary, where the boundary starts as E and is replaced at each step by the preimage of the old boundary together with the centre. It further asserts that X' is smooth over k, that the pulled-back ideal I·O_{X'} is locally generated by one nonzerodivisor, that the reduced zero locus of I·O_{X'} is a simple normal crossings divisor, and that s is an isomorphism over the complement of the zero locus of I.
a.notation: X smooth over k with char k = 0, I ≠ 0 on every component, E snc ⟹ ∃ s from X' to X, a composite of blowups along smooth centres that are snc with the accumulated boundary, with X' smooth, I·O_{X'} invertible with snc support, and s an isomorphism over X ∖ V(I)
a.classical_name: Principalisation of ideal sheaves (Hironaka, in the algorithmic form of Bierstone–Milman, Villamayor, Włodarczyk and Kollár)
a.classical: Let X be a smooth scheme of finite type over a field of characteristic zero, I an ideal sheaf that is nonzero on every irreducible component and E a simple normal crossings divisor. Then there is a finite sequence of blowups along smooth centres lying over the cosupport of I, each with simple normal crossings with the accumulated exceptional divisors and the transform of E, such that I·O_{X'} is the ideal sheaf of a divisor whose support together with the exceptional divisors and the transform of E has simple normal crossings, and the composite is an isomorphism over the complement of the cosupport of I. Reference is J. Kollár, Lectures on Resolution of Singularities, Annals of Mathematics Studies 166, 2007, Chapter 3.
differences: The Lean statement requires X to have one constant relative dimension d over k, while the published theorem allows smooth schemes whose components have different dimensions.
The Lean statement does not require the centres to lie over the zero locus of I, although its isomorphism clause still forces the composite to be an isomorphism away from that locus.

The Lean conclusion asserts simple normal crossings for the support of I·O_{X'} alone and for each centre with the boundary, but not for the union of that support with the final boundary, which the published theorem gives.
The Lean statement omits the functoriality of principalisation with respect to smooth morphisms and field extensions that Kollár's version includes.
a.why: Every Lean clause follows from the standard principalisation theorem with boundary, since an invertible ideal with snc support on a regular scheme is locally a monomial in a regular system of parameters, but the theorem exists in several versions with different boundary clauses and the comparison relies on the project's local definitions of snc centres and blowups.

b.states: For every field k of characteristic zero, every scheme X smooth of relative dimension d, quasi-compact and separated over k, every ideal sheaf I on X whose zero set contains no irreducible component of X, and every closed set E that has simple normal crossings at each of its points, the Lean text asserts that there are X', a morphism s from X' to X and a closed set E' of X'. The morphism s is a composite of blowups along centres that are smooth over k and have simple normal crossings with the current boundary, where the boundary starts as E and after each blowup becomes the preimage of the old boundary together with the centre. Moreover X' is smooth over k, the pullback of I to X' is an invertible ideal sheaf, the reduced zero set of this pullback has simple normal crossings, and s is an isomorphism over the complement of the zero set of I.
b.classical_name: Hironaka's principalisation of ideal sheaves in characteristic zero, in the embedded form with a normal crossings boundary
differences: The Lean statement asks only that the support of the pulled-back ideal have simple normal crossings by itself, while the published theorem makes the pulled-back ideal a divisor that has simple normal crossings together with the final boundary of exceptional divisors and the transform of E.
The Lean statement leaves out the functoriality under smooth morphisms and field extensions that the modern published versions include.
The Lean statement does not require each centre to lie over the zero set of I, although it requires the composite to be an isomorphism over the complement of that zero set.
The Lean statement asks X to have one relative dimension d and to be separated, while the published theorem allows any smooth scheme of finite type over k.
The Lean statement requires X to be smooth of one relative dimension d and separated over k, while the published theorem allows any smooth scheme of finite type over k.
The Lean statement does not require each centre to lie over the zero set of I, although IsIso (s ∣_ I.support.compl) forces the composite to be an isomorphism over the complement of that zero set.

The Lean conclusion gives simple normal crossings for the reduced support of I·O_X' alone, while the published theorem gives simple normal crossings for that support together with the final boundary of exceptional divisors and the transform of E.
The Lean statement leaves out the functoriality under smooth morphisms and field extensions that the published versions of Kollár and others include.

a.states: Let S be a Noetherian scheme all of whose local rings are integrally closed domains, and let U be a dense open subset of S. Let G and H be group schemes over S that are semi-abelian in the project's sense, which means commutative, smooth, separated, quasi-compact and geometrically connected over S, with the pullback to every geometric point Spec Ω → S an extension of an abelian variety by a split torus whose character group is free of finite rank. Then every homomorphism of group schemes f from G_U to H_U over U is the restriction to U of exactly one homomorphism of group schemes F from G to H over S.
a.notation: S normal Noetherian, U ⊆ S dense open, G, H semi-abelian over S ⟹ ∀ f ∈ Hom_{U-gr}(G_U, H_U) ∃! F ∈ Hom_{S-gr}(G, H) with F|_U = f
a.classical_name: Extension of homomorphisms of semi-abelian schemes over a normal base (Faltings and Chai)
a.classical: Let S be a normal Noetherian scheme, U ⊆ S a dense open subscheme and G, H semi-abelian schemes over S, that is smooth separated commutative group schemes of finite type whose fibres are extensions of abelian varieties by tori. Then every homomorphism G_U → H_U extends uniquely to a homomorphism G → H. The reference is G. Faltings and C.-L. Chai, Degeneration of Abelian Varieties, Springer 1990, Chapter I, Proposition 2.7.
differences: The project asks for the torus extension at every geometric point and with a split torus, while Faltings and Chai ask for it on every fibre with an arbitrary torus, and the two conditions agree because a torus over an algebraically closed field is split and the maximal torus of a smooth connected commutative group descends to the residue field.

The project asks for a smooth, separated and quasi-compact structure morphism where Faltings and Chai ask for a smooth separated group scheme of finite type, and these agree because smoothness already includes local finite presentation.
a.why: Every hypothesis on S, U, G and H and the existence and uniqueness in the conclusion match the statement of Faltings and Chai once the fibre condition is read geometrically.

b.states: For every Noetherian scheme S in universe 0 whose stalks are all integrally closed domains and every dense open subset U of S, the statement takes two group objects G and H over S that are semi-abelian. Semi-abelian is defined as commutative, smooth, separated, quasi-compact and geometrically connected over S, with the pullback to every geometric point an extension of an abelian variety by a split torus, where the quotient map is a flat, surjective and quasi-compact homomorphism whose kernel, as a pullback square over the unit section, is the split torus. For every homomorphism of group objects f from the restriction of G over U to the restriction of H over U, the statement asserts that exactly one homomorphism of group objects F from G to H over S restricts to f over U.
b.classical_name: Extension of homomorphisms of semi-abelian schemes over a normal Noetherian base (Faltings and Chai, Degeneration of Abelian Varieties, Chapter I, Proposition 2.7)
differences: The Lean text quantifies only over schemes in universe 0 and over geometric points whose fields lie in universe 0, which is a formal restriction without mathematical effect.

Moret-Bailly, Pinceaux de variétés abéliennes, Astérisque 129, 1985, Chapter I.

a.states: Let g be a prime, d a positive integer and K a field with an F_g-algebra structure of dimension d, so that K is a field with g^d elements. For regular θ and θ′ it claims τ(θ) = τ(θ′) exactly when θ′ = θ^{g^i} for some i < d. Finally it claims that every irreducible character of GL_d(F_g) with these vanishing averages, which is the project's notion of a cuspidal character, equals τ(θ) for some regular θ.

a.classical: For a prime power q and n ≥ 1, the irreducible cuspidal characters of GL_n(F_q) correspond bijectively to the Frobenius orbits {θ, θ^q, …, θ^{q^{n−1}}} of regular characters θ of F_{q^n}^×. The character attached to θ has degree ∏_{i=1}^{n−1}(q^i − 1) and value (−1)^{n−1} ∑_{i=0}^{n−1} θ(z^{q^i}) at an element whose eigenvalues z, z^q, …, z^{q^{n−1}} generate F_{q^n}, and Green's paper determines its values on all conjugacy classes. The reference is J. A. Green, The characters of the finite general linear groups, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 80, 1955.
differences: The Lean text treats only the prime fields F_g, while Green's theorem covers GL_n(F_q) for every prime power q.
The Lean text fixes the values of τ(θ) only at the identity and at elements with irreducible characteristic polynomial, while Green gives the values on every conjugacy class.

The project's cuspidality condition checks only the standard maximal parabolic subgroups and does so through the average of the character over their unipotent radicals, which is equivalent to the usual condition that the unipotent radical of every proper parabolic subgroup fixes no nonzero vector.
a.why: The degree, the elliptic values, the identification modulo Frobenius and the surjectivity onto cuspidal characters each match the standard statement, and the restriction to prime fields is explicit because the group is GL_d over the integers modulo the prime g.

b.states: For every prime g, every d > 0 and every field K that is an algebra of dimension d over ZMod g, the statement asserts a map τ from characters θ of the multiplicative group of K to complex functions on GL_d(ZMod g). For regular θ and θ' the equality τθ = τθ' holds exactly when θ' = θ^(g^i) for some i < d. Every cuspidal irreducible character equals τθ for some regular θ.

a.states: Let k be a finite field, n a natural number and ψ₀ a nontrivial additive character of k. Let ρ be a finite-dimensional irreducible complex representation of GL_{n+1}(k) that is cuspidal, meaning that for every proper standard parabolic subgroup the unipotent radical fixes no nonzero vector. Then the restriction of ρ to the mirabolic subgroup P of matrices with last row (0, …, 0, 1) is isomorphic to the representation of P induced from the character u ↦ ψ₀(u_{12} + u_{23} + ⋯ + u_{n,n+1}) of the upper unitriangular group U.

Then the restriction of π to the mirabolic subgroup P_n is isomorphic to Ind_{U_n}^{P_n} ψ, which is irreducible. The reference is S. I. Gelfand, Representations of the full linear group over a finite field, Mathematics of the USSR Sbornik 12, 1970.

a.states: For every number field E and algebraic closure Ω of E there is a group homomorphism art from the idele group of E to the quotient of Gal(Ω/E) by the closure of its commutator subgroup. The map art is continuous, surjective and open, and its kernel is the closure of the subgroup generated by E^× and the identity component of the infinite ideles. Let v be a finite place and A a valuation ring of Ω above v. An element is the image of a unit of E_v exactly when it is the image of an inertia element of A. It is the image of a uniformizer of E_v exactly when it is the image of σ^{−1} for some σ in the decomposition group of A that acts as x ↦ x^{Nv} on the residue field, and the closure of the image of E_v^× is the image of the decomposition group of A.

This homomorphism therefore maps O_v^× onto the inertia group and a uniformizer to a Frobenius element modulo inertia, and its image on E_v^× is dense in the decomposition group. J. Tate, Global class field theory, in J. W. S. Cassels and A. Fröhlich, Algebraic Number Theory (1967).

a.states: Let V be a Noetherian ring and A an abelian scheme over Spec V, that is, a commutative group scheme that is smooth and proper with geometrically connected fibres. Let L be a line bundle on A that is relatively ample, which means that over each affine open U of Spec V some power L^N embeds A_U as a closed subscheme of a projective space over U. Then there is a closed subscheme Z of A that is finite and flat over V. For every V-scheme T, a point x ∈ A(T) factors through Z exactly when the line bundle t_x^*L ⊗ pr₂^*L^{−1} on T ×_V A is trivial over T' ×_V A for each member T' of some open cover of T. In other words Z represents the functor K(L) of points whose translation preserves L up to a bundle from the base.

If L is relatively ample then φ_L is an isogeny, so K(L) is a finite flat group scheme over S. D. Mumford, J. Fogarty and F. Kirwan, Geometric Invariant Theory, Chapter 6 (1994).

It then asserts the existence of a closed immersion from a scheme Z into A with Z finite and flat over Spec V. The scheme Z is required to represent K(L), in the sense that a T-point x of A factors through Z exactly when the line bundle m_x*L ⊗ pr₂*L⁻¹ on T ×_V A is trivial over a neighbourhood of every point of T.

a.states: Let R be a discrete valuation ring with perfect residue field and fraction field K, Ω a separable closure of K, and V a valuation ring of Ω lying over R, with inertia group I_V ⊂ Gal(Ω/K). Potential good reduction means that there are a finite extension L/K and a discrete valuation ring W with fraction field L lying over R such that A_L is the generic fibre of an abelian scheme over W, as a group scheme.

a.classical_name: Serre–Tate criterion for potential good reduction
a.classical: Let K be a field with a discrete valuation, A an abelian variety over K and l a prime different from the residue characteristic. Then A has potential good reduction if and only if the image of the inertia group in Aut(T_l A) is finite, which follows from the Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich criterion. J.-P. Serre and J. Tate, Good reduction of abelian varieties, Annals of Mathematics 88 (1968).

b.states: For every discrete valuation ring R with perfect residue field, its fraction field K, a separable closure Ω of K and a valuation subring V of Ω with V ∩ K = R, every abelian variety A over K and every prime l that is nonzero in the residue field of R, the statement asserts an equivalence. a.classical_name: Harish-Chandra's correspondence between closed invariant subspaces and (g,K)-submodules

Knapp, Representation Theory of Semisimple Groups, An Overview Based on Examples, 1986, Chapter VIII.

Line bundles are encoded by Čech cocycle data on open covers and isomorphisms by global generators of the quotient bundle, which is a way of writing the usual notion.

a.states: The proposition is the conjunction of two statements about a noetherian ring R that is complete and separated for the I-adic topology of an ideal I. The first says that if X is proper over R and Z is separated, locally of finite type and quasi-compact over R, then every family of R-morphisms f_e from the thickenings X_e = X ×_R R/I^{e+1} to Z that is compatible with the inclusions X_e → X_{e+1} comes from a unique R-morphism g from X to Z. The second says that if Y_e are proper R/I^{e+1}-schemes with Y_e = Y_{e+1} ×_{R/I^{e+2}} R/I^{e+1} through maps β_e, and N_e are line bundles on Y_e with N_e ≅ β_e^*N_{e+1} and N_0 relatively ample over R/I, then there are a proper R-scheme X with a relatively ample line bundle M and compatible identifications Y_e ≅ X ×_R R/I^{e+1} under which N_e is isomorphic to the pullback of M for every e.

a.classical: Let A be a noetherian ring complete for the I-adic topology and Y = Spec A. If X is proper and Z is separated of finite type over Y, then Hom_Y(X, Z) → Hom(X̂, Ẑ) is bijective, and if X̂ is a proper formal scheme over the completion of Y with an invertible sheaf L̂ whose reduction to X_0 is ample, then there are a projective Y-scheme X and an ample invertible sheaf L whose completions are X̂ and L̂. A standard reference is A. Grothendieck, Éléments de géométrie algébrique III, première partie, Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS 11, 1961, Theorems 5.4.1 and 5.4.5.
differences: The Lean statement describes formal schemes and their line bundles as inverse systems of thickenings and of line bundles with level-wise isomorphisms that need not be chosen compatibly, which is harmless because any choice of these isomorphisms gives an inverse system.
The second Lean part concludes that X is proper with a relatively ample line bundle in place of projective, which is equivalent over a noetherian affine base.

Relative ampleness is defined by asking that over each affine open of the base some positive tensor power has finitely many sections whose non-vanishing loci are affine, cover the scheme and have coordinate rings generated by the quotients of the sections, which is relative very ampleness of a power and matches the usual notion.
a.why: Both parts restate EGA III 5.4.1 and 5.4.5 for an I-adically complete noetherian ring in the language of adic systems, and the encodings of line bundles and of ampleness match the usual notions.
